speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Change is the only constant, they say, and with our Public Service, it, too, will be busy evolving, moving forward and making adaptations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore’s sustainability depends very much on the ability of our Public Service to do this and to keep relevant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This will be crucial to take Singapore through the current generation and into the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The officers will need to face head-on technological disruptions with a renewed mindset and perspective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They will need to keep abreast as they will be leading society through policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: To negotiate the changes, they must top up their capabilities, be change makers and embark on continuous education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They must be able to, what I would call, learn, unlearn and relearn, as needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Learn and relearn is quite obvious, but the ability to unlearn is important, too, so as not to be stuck in old school ways of doing things.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Versatility and agility will be the words of the day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Moreover, with the more discerning public and highly-educated younger generation with higher expectations, the effectiveness and efficiency of the Public Service, as defined today, will certainly need a review and a relook.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How will they be upskilled with deeper and more sophisticated digital capabilities?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The day before, I spoke about Singapore as a thriving hub in the Pacific Century.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While the current external conditions are favourable, Singapore’s continued growth will largely depend on whether we are able to stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: An ageing population, shrinking workforce, international competition and technological disruption – as has been discussed in this House – and other unforeseen calamity could set us back, especially if we are unprepared, unable to adapt and unable to reinvent ourselves.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While these risk factors are not unique to Singapore, our responses can be.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: But we will have to face them squarely in order to find solutions to address them.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: To do so requires courage, imagination, discipline and organisation.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Singapore has one of the most efficient Public Service systems in the world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: But past achievements are no guarantee for future success.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: We cannot allow efficiency to be replaced by bureaucracy, urgency by complacency and creativity by paralysis.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Could we expect the Public Service to lead change?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, many of the issues we face today are complex and multifaceted in nature.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For instance, I spoke about the need to nurture a multilingual environment for Singaporeans to use their mother tongues frequently and naturally.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: If this idea is accepted, whose responsibility would it be to see to the creation of such an environment?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How would a wide range of solutions be coordinated amongst different agencies responsible for service delivery?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How would the service glean the world's best practices for our own learning?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Would our service invest in its own research and development (R&D) as part of a smart Government?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At times, I feel the role of the Public Service has become that of a marketer – successfully meeting consumer expectations – no longer one-way, top-down, nor linear.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, we ought to bear in mind that these are our fellow citizens and not consumers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is not a one-shot game where we carry out a transaction, make them happy and not worry about their long-term interests or their relationship with us as a community.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Remembering that the Public Service builds public value, and that we share a common interest with all Singaporeans, we need to care for them and not treat them as in a transactional relationship.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to redesign our service and map the citizen journey around key values which we all share, not just the pursuit of bureaucratic goals and departmental interests, but also, not populist demands or individual outcry.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Likewise, the way we serve citizens will also need to change to keep up with the times, as well as our changing demographics.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For one, our senior citizens might not be as savvy as our digital natives.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But we must cater to all segments of society and continue to deliver to everyone the services they need in ways most natural to them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, how can our Public Service continue to evolve so that we deliver the best services we can to our citizens, and that our public officers can remain effective in their roles?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Their work gets harder each year with rising expectations from the public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can PMO consider putting in place internal quality service managers (QSMs) to look into and ensure that feedback from public servants is looked into?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can PMO also ensure that all public servants have direct communication channels with the top management through regular and frequent all-hands meetings and through pigeon-hole sessions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should also better recognise public servant contributions and skills beyond their formal academic qualifications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And we need to ensure they work in an environment where they can develop and apply rules in a more flexible way, so as to better serve Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that this is the same for all Ministries and Statutory Boards and I would be glad to be proven wrong in saying that public servants fear speaking up.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, policymakers and lawmakers may not be able to foresee gaps and unintended consequences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It will build confidence that policies were not being rushed and that citizens could participate meaningfully in policymaking.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would divide my discussion into two parts: the pre-Parliament stage and the Parliament stage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are many positive examples of public consultations where a Ministry would publicise the consultation and invite public comments on draft legislation, after which it publishes a summary of the comments received and the Ministry's responses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It goes without saying that the consultation period should give sufficient time for people to respond.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was sensible then that the Ministry extended the consultation period after request from the public.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In recent times, there were instances when laws seemed to be rushed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, the Administration of Justice (Protection) Bill was only put up on the feedback unit Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH) portal after it was presented in Parliament for First Reading and a petition filed on this Bill was somehow not sent to the Public Petitions Committee.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While a Ministry may certainly choose to adopt other methods of consultation, for example, closed-door focus groups or stakeholder discussions, I would say that this should not replace an open consultation on the actual Bill if the Government wants to have a bigger buy-in, especially in controversial matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There seems to me some scope for improvement, too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Regarding the explanatory statement to Bills, sometimes, we find explanatory statements that simply repeat the wording of the Bill without explaining how the clauses will improve things.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, we do see some more helpful explanatory statements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A recent example is the Public Sector (Governance) Bill where it was stated that the clause setting out the Minister's powers over public bodies was necessary due to inconsistencies in existing legislation and to avoid duplication.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Here, an attempt is made to give a reason for the new law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One useful initiative is the ongoing pilot by the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) to show the changes made by Bills in tracked mode, but I believe this is currently only available to MPs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I hope this can be available to the public to facilitate greater understanding of changes made.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was rejected by the Court of Appeal as invalid because nowhere in the Second Reading speech of the Minister was Parliament told that the Act was intended to apply to persons who were not human beings and not vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, at the same time, they have also talked about how they tend to be aloof and clinical.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They understand that there is a lot of work that the Public Service has to do but they cannot understand why the Public Service cannot understand them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think there is a disconnect, and it is this disconnect that we need to address.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Also, as our society evolves and the needs and demands become more complex, the voices become louder and people are more sophisticated.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, the Public Service has to keep up.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As the world changes and we enter into Industry 4.0 with innovation and change, we need to keep up, we need to know what is happening and we need to be ahead.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But the concern has always been whether our Public Service is afraid to change because we have been so successful, and whether or not, if we change, the success formulae might be tweaked to our own detriment.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I filed this cut to ask a few questions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The ruling party aside, our continued growth and bonding and success as a country continue to depend on this machinery frequently referred to as the "zheng hu" (in Hokkien) which is, in effect, the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, while I understand also, before I go into that, Sir, the need for a rotation, it breaks the continuity of management and responses to issues.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It may also inhibit a vigorous review of a predecessor's initiative or the work of a team under that predecessor.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on to my questions, Sir, what efforts have been undertaken by the Public Service to understand ground sentiments, address misapprehensions and implement policies in line with declared intent conveyed through Ministerial speeches?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: What are the agencies that have recognised within the last five years the necessity to change their operating mindsets and models?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: How did the recognition come about and how have such changes been implemented?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: What are the results of such changes and what is the public perception?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: How does the Government achieve buy-in from civil servants on the ground in the shaping and implementation of policies initiated from top management and Ministers?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I ask these questions because I think it is important that if there are changes and there are good effective changes, these should be effectively and properly communicated to the citizenry.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: We have the Public Service Commission (PSC), which has, over the years, helped build an efficient, honest and talented Public Service sector.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Nevertheless, there are some areas that our public sector needs to pay close attention to.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Citizens are also now expecting more from governments as innovation and the Internet of Things (IoT) in the private sector have enhanced many of their experiences.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: More importantly, other governments have leap-frogged and have improved their interactions with their citizens with the advent of new technologies.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Therefore, our public sector, good as they are, must also up its game.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It behooves the Government to deploy resources productively and, indeed, to innovate almost as a habit, and at every citizen and enterprise touchpoint.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The private sector offers some good examples of how this can be done, such as centralised procurement and also shared service centres.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: With centralised procurement through aggregating demand across Ministries and agencies, cost savings can be had.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Shared service centre, in the areas of information technology (IT), human resources (HR), finance, facility management and so on, can also provide significant productivity benefits as there is standardisation of processes as well as economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I applaud this effort and look forward to hearing from the Minister an update on this very interesting project.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Another area which is often in the way of innovation is policies, rules and regulations.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Some of these are necessary and remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: But many are out-of-date and are in need of urgent review.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Chairman, being part of an efficient Public Service also involves cutting red tape and unnecessary bureaucracy.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Internally, it avoids officers being bogged down by unnecessary administration instead of focusing on higher value-added work.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leon Perera, you can take both cuts together.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I ask this because many whistleblowers in any organisation may hesitate to complain to a department within their organisation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, each year, Government Ministries and Statutory Boards produce annual reports.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In some cases, printed copies are sent to various stakeholders, including Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not sure how many of these printed copies are retained by the recipients for long.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Users can print these for their own use if they want to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since they have to print for the printing themselves, it is likely that they would only print the pages they need.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would save the Government money and it is greener, with few implications for the wider public.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some other countries have formalised guidelines to minimise printing of Government annual reports.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the New South Wales government in Australia goes so far as to say that government departments and, I quote, "may only externally print hardcopies where express permission is granted by the relevant Minister following clear justification on need and demand".

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In working together, the Deputy Prime Minister highlighted that the digital and future economy can drive growth, innovation and productivity.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Digitalisation will transform the way we work and deliver public services and create many new economic opportunities.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is important for the Public Service to continue to evolve and reinvent itself to meet the needs of Singaporeans today and in the future.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is imperative that the Public Service attract the right talent and retain them so as to better prepare the rest of the workers for digitalisation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, we can look forward to more citizen-centric services through the use of technologies, such as data science and analytics, thereby transforming our Public Service delivery.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Within the public sector, there is a need to transform processes and strengthen digital capabilities of our public agencies, the employees and Singaporeans as a whole.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While the public sector embarks on this journey, there must also be parallel efforts to ensure that the public servants as well as Singaporeans at large are not left out, especially those who are mature and seniors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Essentially, they must also be willing to be behind this change.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Public Service, being the largest employer, must ensure Public Service employees are also given appropriate training to adopt, adapt and stay relevant for future jobs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: No one can escape the waves of change in the digital world.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, important that the Public Service and its agencies keep up to the speed of change.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Public Service and its agencies, too, should take stock of jobs at risk and future jobs in demand so as to ensure that workers of today and tomorrow are placed in future jobs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am contented to hear that the Public Service is taking the lead to invest in strategic capabilities, such as digital, data, engineering.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What are some of the capabilities built in the Public Service to prepare Singapore towards the digital economy?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: One of the strategies under the Committee of the Future Economy is to build strong digital capabilities.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What are the future plans to further build such capabilities within our Public Service to enhance delivery of public services to our citizens?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On the whole, how is the Public Service responding to technological disruption?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That was a vigorous debate in which many Members of the House took part and was one of the few times the Workers' Party put forward an alternative proposal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, in the course of the debate, it emerged that, in fact, the differences between parties were relatively narrow and the benchmark salaries derived from both calculations would not be that different, notwithstanding different approaches to calculation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The principle was that money should not be a disincentive to serve but it certainly should not be the main incentive.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, the salaries of other public appointment holders were set at specified fractions of the Ministerial salary benchmark.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, salaries cannot be set in stone, as income levels and Government expenditure change over time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The White Paper recommended this benchmark be reviewed every five years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the 2015 Committee of Supply debate, my colleague Mr Edwin Tong had asked PMO about whether it was time to review the benchmark with the five-year mark approaching.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At that time, Deputy Prime Minister Teo mentioned that he did not feel the benchmark needed to be reviewed and commented that it had worked well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Well, it is now 2018, after the five-year timeline to review what the White Paper had recommended.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, in 2012, the Parliament debated and endorsed the White Paper on "Salaries for a Capable and Committed Government", which consists of recommendations from the Ministerial Salaries Review Committee.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Among the recommendations, the Committee recommended that the salary framework be reviewed every five years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If there was, indeed, a recent review done, what are the recommendations and whether there will be adjustments made to the Ministerial salaries as per the framework established?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore needs good leaders, leaders that can steer the country to the forefront of innovation, create opportunities for growth, delicately manoeuvre the path of diplomacy to ensure the nation’s continued survival.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To achieve that, we need capable, dedicated men and women of integrity to step up to the plate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But how do we attract these people, who often are already established or are establishing a steady career path, to forgo their attractive remuneration, perks and benefits to join the Government?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Political service and public service require sacrifice, and many of our past and present Ministers are good examples of this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most importantly, we have been practising a system that promotes transparency with no hidden perks.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These principles have been the cornerstone of our Government, which has always espoused a clean and transparent governance model.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But there is a need to be realistic as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While many heads of banks, industries and businesses often earn more than our Ministers in terms of salaries, bonuses, perks and allowances because of their responsibilities, our public officeholders, who handle Ministries with larger budgets and an even greater impact on the country and the population, should also be paid fairly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The details were laid out earlier by our hon Member Mr Vikram Nair and I will not repeat them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is, therefore, perhaps opportune for the Deputy Prime Minister to update if a review has been conducted and adjustments, if any, will be made to this benchmark?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government has also launched the SkillsFuture programme to equip Singaporeans with skills for future jobs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As we create new jobs which require new skills in the industries, the public agencies must also correspondingly upgrade and deepen the skills of public officers to better serve the public and business community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: With digitalisation and emerging technologies, public agencies should also adopt these technologies to further improve their productivity, efficiency and customer service.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the years, many Government agencies have outsourced part of their services to private service providers in areas, such as project management, facilities management, management of public hotlines and so on.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the process, some public agencies have lost expertise or capabilities in these areas, thus resulting in some lapses, as highlighted by our annual Auditor-General's findings.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to relook into the skills required by our public officers to better manage outsourced projects or services so as to achieve better public accountability in using public funds.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the same time, the public agencies must set up systems to be interfaced with industry practices.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, the introduction of the Building Information System (BIM) for building projects by the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) sets the pace for the digitalisation of building designs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I feel that these are good initiatives and convey an encouraging message to current and future officers that they can aspire to a fulfilling career in the various public agencies regardless of their academic qualifications, as long as they have the required skillsets and can contribute well in their roles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: This is consistent with the larger SkillsFuture movement which calls for the private sector to look beyond paper qualifications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: The Public Service should also respond to the call, given it is the largest single employer in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Are there concrete examples on how these initiatives have benefited individual officers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Are there also examples of officers who have progressed well in their careers based on good performance and skills, despite not having traditional academic qualifications?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Given technological disruptions, many organisations both within the public and private sectors have gone digital and their workplaces have been transformed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We must be prepared for these changes, given that the Public Service is the largest single employer in Singapore and should thus set a good example for other employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The way we serve citizens would also need to change to keep up with the times.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We see a few good initiatives, for example, parking.sg, self-help e-services from various major agencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: All these changes would mean that the internal working environment within the agencies will need to change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Chairman, before I begin on the work of the Public Service, let me address the points raised by Members Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Alex Yam on the salary framework for political officeholders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The current framework is based on the 2012 White Paper on salaries for capable and committed Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Members may recall that the Prime Minister appointed an independent committee in May 2011 to review the basis and level of political salaries to help ensure an honest and competent Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The committee's recommendations contained in the White Paper were thoroughly debated over three days in this House and endorsed in January 2012.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The endorsed salary framework was implemented with effect from May 2011.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I last updated this House on this subject during the 2015 Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I had informed the House that the salary framework was working well and that the Government was maintaining the salary level established by the 2011 Review Committee.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The 2011 committee had suggested reviewing the salary scheme after five years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In line with this, the Prime Minister formed a fresh committee last year to review whether the salary framework remains appropriate and valid against its intended goals and what adjustments may be useful, and whether there is a need to adjust the salaries should there be a change in overall salary levels based on the proposed framework.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Prime Minister has written to the committee to thank the committee for its work and the well-considered recommendations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Chairman, the 2017 committee comprises nine members headed by the 2011 committee chairman, Mr Gerard Ee.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The other eight members were Dr Abdul Razak Omar, Mr Thomas Chua, Mrs Fang Ai Lian, Ms Eu Lin Goh, Mr Stephen Lee, Ms Mary Liu, Mr Ramasamy Dhinakaran and Mrs Mildred Tan.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These independent members are experienced and well-established in a range of sectors: social and community service, business, trade union and professional services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Two of these eight members, Mrs Fang Ai Lian and Mr Stephen Lee, served on the 2011 committee while six were new.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In 2017, the committee reviewed the salary framework and submitted its views and recommendations to the Prime Minister in December last year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, the committee reaffirmed that the current salary framework laid out in the 2012 White Paper is a simple and effective salary framework for political appointment holders and MPs and remains true to the three key principles which this House had arrived at through consensus in 2012.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In fact, this consensus on the principles included Members of the Opposition party.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These three principles were: (a) salaries must be competitive so that people of the right calibre are not deterred from stepping forward to lead the country; (b) the ethos of political service entails making sacrifices and, hence, there should be a discount in the pay formula; and (c) there should be a clean wage with no hidden perks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The salaries should be linked to the individual performance of political appointment holders and the socioeconomic progress of Singapore Citizens.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The 2017 committee affirmed that these principles remain relevant and should be retained.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These principles form the cornerstone of a system that ensures competitive salaries while maintaining transparency and accountability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Second, the committee assessed that the current salary benchmark strikes a good balance between paying competitive salaries and displaying the ethos of political service and recommends continuing the use of this benchmark to determine the total annual salary of a Minister at a grade of MR4.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The salary benchmark which is based on the medium income of the top 1,000 earners who are Singapore Citizens reflects the calibre of the people Singapore needs for good Government while the 40% discount from this signifies the ethos of political service.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Third, the committee recommended retaining the current pay structure for political appointment holders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The committee assessed that the structure is simple and easy to understand.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There are direct links to individual performance and national outcomes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: All salary components are clearly spelt out with no hidden benefits and all salary components are within the benchmark.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In particular, the committee reviewed the existing indicators in the National Bonus framework and recommended retaining them as they adequately covered the spectrum of the Government's efforts at the macro level.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The National Bonus is linked to real gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate which tracks how well Singapore is growing economically as a country and unemployment rate of Singapore Citizens which tracks whether growth translates to jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The income-related indicators reflect whether jobs translate to better income for all Singaporeans, including average and lower-wage workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, the committee has also recommended a few adjustments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: One, to adjust political salaries annually in line with annual benchmark movements.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The committee has affirmed that the current salary structure for political appointment holders, including the National Bonus framework, remains relevant and sound.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The economy is going through a period of transition and the Government has decided to watch the changing economic conditions and outlook further rather than making any refinements now.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The 2017 committee has reviewed and reaffirmed the key principles that form the underlying basis for determining political salaries.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The committee is also of the view that the existing salary framework remains relevant and sound in ensuring a flow of capable leaders committed to the continued success of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Government will, of course, keep this House fully informed of any changes to the salary structure or level.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I have taken Members through the substance of the views and recommendations from the committee.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Government is releasing the Review Committee's report.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Now, Mr Chairman, let me thank the Members for their views and their continued support for the work of our public officers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Over the past few days, Members debated how to position Singapore on a firmer footing for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are progressing well on our economic transformation, with the Public Service working closely with industry, our unions and workers to deepen their skills and prepare for the future.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The PMO-Strategy Group is working closely with our agencies and other central agencies, such as the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service Division (PSD), to adopt a systems approach to planning and coordination.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This includes areas, such as scenario planning, budget, manpower, population, land, security, climate change and new opportunities in the Digital and Future Economy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have formed the Smart Nation and Digital Government Group last May to accelerate our Smart Nation efforts.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Mr Lee Yi Shyan cited demographic challenges which stem from our low total fertility rate (TFR).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Agencies have worked together to strengthen our support for marriage and parenthood in the key areas of housing, preschool and support in the workplace and the community.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Minister Josephine Teo will give an update of our population priorities and strategies to ensure that we are well-prepared for the future later on during this COS for PMO.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Climate change is also a whole-of-nation issue where all countries need to take action now to safeguard our collective future.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Together with other countries, Singapore will do our part to reduce our emissions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To do so in a cost-effective manner, the carbon tax is a decisive move.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Its merits were discussed extensively during the Budget Debate.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The transition period and support will help our companies and consumers make the adjustments.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Minister Masagos Zulkifli will provide more details in his speech on our implementation plans in the COS for Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources (MEWR).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Singapore needs to remain economically competitive and be a smart, green and liveable city with opportunities for Singaporeans of all ages.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As Mr Sean Kian Peng and Mr Lee Yi Shyan pointed out, technological progress and increasing digitisation are effecting rapid changes globally.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Minister Vivian Balakrishnan will provide a progress update and outline new Smart Nation initiatives.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will help our people and our companies make adjustments for the future and continue to raise the capabilities of our public officers to deliver better public services.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is what a Caring, Competent and Trusted Public Service has to do, and what many Members, such as Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Seah Kian Peng, Mr Lee Yi Shyan, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Cedric Foo, Ms Chia Yong Yong and Dr Teo Ho Pin, have suggested.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will continue to strengthen our institutions to operate in a more integrated way.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The recently passed Public Sector Governance Act strengthens our corporate governance and accountability.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about our internal framework for reporting wrongdoings, and this is an internal disclosure framework.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The number has remained stable over the last three years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Of these, about nine in 10 were followed up by formal investigations, with 134 resulting in some form of disciplinary action.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, many of these cases did not involve the misuse of public funds and did not reflect serious gaps in the Public Service's systems of checks and controls.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, the system is there, it works well, public officers are aware of it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And, as I have said before, there are also avenues for public officers to report to the PSC or also to the Head of the Civil Service and our enforcement agencies, including the Police and the CPIB, and Mr Leon Perera knows that these are very effective organisations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On annual reports, I completely agree with Mr Leon Perera.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We should only print them when we need to.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, this is the policy that we adopt, and I take the suggestions to heart and we will see how we can reduce publication of physical copies further.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Lee Yi Shyan also cited the intensified competition among Asian economies and asked how we could adopt an innovation culture more widely.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Public Service will continue to help and partner Singaporeans and companies to seize new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As the various sectors of our economy are transforming for the future, the Public Service has also embarked on its own transformation to be more innovative, work smarter through technology and deliver better public services for our people.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung will speak more on the transformation effort later but, here, I would like to highlight two areas.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin, Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Mr Lee Yi Shyan asked how the Public Service as a whole is upgrading and reinventing itself.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: All our agencies are working on enhancing their digital capabilities, which will allow them to deliver more integrated services for Singaporeans and businesses.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: An example is the new Housing and Development Board (HDB) Resale Portal.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Real estate agents benefit from this, too, as they can also free up the time they spend on administrative work and focus on offering more value-added services for their clients and, of course, members of the public benefit when they are doing resale flat transactions, whether they are buyers or sellers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will elaborate on our Digital Government efforts later.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Ms Thanaletchimi and Dr Teo Ho Pin also asked what the Public Service will do to prepare our workforce for technological disruption.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We also support our officers of all ages to transform, upskill and innovate, so that they are ready to take on new roles.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is also a question that Mr Patrick Tay asked.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS), for example, more than 400 staff ambassadors, called LEverage Analytics, Design and Digitalisation (LEA:D) Advocates, support their peers through change and learning new skills.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Several LEA:D Advocates are 55 years and older.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They have stepped forward to share with others how they have picked up new digital skills to analyse large volumes of data and digital applications to automate data entry.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin rightly pointed out that, ultimately, building a tech-enabled workforce is not an end in itself.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It must benefit our citizens through more effective delivery of services.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To maximise the benefits and savings, operating models and business processes must also be re-engineered and jobs redesigned so that our officers can immediately put their new skills to use.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, let me thank Members once again for their strong support for the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, every industry is undergoing transformation and disruption.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Transformation is not new to the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: From computerisation in the 1980s, the Public Service (PS)21 Movement in the 1990s, the Public Service has pushed itself to change with the times.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, as Deputy Prime Minister Teo mentioned, we will need to find opportunities amidst the challenges of technological disruption and slowing workforce growth.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The question is: what areas should we focus on?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To answer that question, let me first talk about the state of the Public Service today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It continues to uphold the values of honesty and integrity, strives to serve the public better, and we are able to attract our fair share of talent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are the critical aspects of a functioning and effective Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It does not happen that way in every country, and it did not happen here just because public officers are yes-men or yes-women.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, Ms Chia is correctly worried that we do not want buy-in to be weakened over time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, what she said is actually the opposite of Mr Louis Ng's concern that public servants are not speaking up and opposing the Government's policy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The system works today because of the mutual trust and respect between Ministers and public officers, which have been built up through years of working together.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Public officers know that national policies are developed in the long-term interest of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ministers have confidence that when they set the policy direction or make a policy speech, the Public Service will back them up with diligent implementation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But public officers are not public figures, so Ministers understand that they have to do the heavy lifting in engaging the populace and speak up for public officers when they are unfairly criticised.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is something that we must continue to work on and not let it be weakened.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Citizen engagement, including co-creation with the public, has been a major focus since Public Sector Transformation started in 2012.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, on Ms Chia Yong Yong’s question again when she asked about whether public servants understand ground sentiments and whether sufficient effort has been put in to engage the ground, the Public Service has, over the year, expanded both digital and community outreach channels.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, the People’s Association (PA) has a Kopi Talk series; the Ministry of Communications and Information's (MCI’s) REACH Listening Points and Facebook Live Chats enable agencies to engage broader segments of society in understanding the people's sentiments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have also been growing our citizen engagement capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These projects include the Ministry of Health's (MOH’s) Citizens’ Jury on Diabetes, and the Singapore Tourism Board’s envisioning exercise for Chinatown and Little India.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To Ms Sylvia Lim's question, it has become the norm for agencies to do public consultations on legislative amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over the past one year, Ministries have done consultations over a wide range of Bills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are very useful exercises to solicit the concerns the public may have on the Bills, or suggestions that can improve both the policy thinking as well as its implementation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In certain circumstances, such as when the Bills are time-sensitive or revisions are routine, a Ministry may decide not to conduct a public consultation exercise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also mentioned that Bills can be better presented and Second Reading speeches can also be improved.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We take note of all that and, as always, we are always striving to improve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another area which the Public Service is continuously improving on is the last mile of service delivery and the touchpoint with the public.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The basic nature of Public Service is that it serves the masses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the first challenge is that service delivery can be impersonal.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, because the system must work for the masses, consistency in application of rules is critical.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Otherwise, we get invidious comparisons between citizen A and citizen B.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the second challenge is that the system can be inflexible and does not cater sufficiently to exceptions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Cedric Foo, Mr Seah Kian Peng and Mr Patrick Tay asked how the Public Service is innovating, raising productivity, especially in the context of technological advancement.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think tackling these two challenges is a good, down-to-earth start.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, our smart phones and apps can communicate with us in an individualised way even though they are automated systems.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a result, the conversations between the CPF officers and the public became richer and more meaningful.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Senior Minister of State Dr Janil Puthucheary will speak more about the efforts we are taking to fully leverage technology to deliver public service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second challenge of inflexibility is much harder to overcome.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It involves tempering a system that is consistent and six sigma reliable by design with the recognition that there are exceptions, rules are not perfect, and human judgement and discretion are needed from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the Public Service, my view is that the key innovation is not so much driven by technology, but by our humanistic instincts to make a sound judgement, to take a bit of risk, to take responsibility for our decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we need to empower middle management, even ground officers, to be able to do that, while ensuring that the integrity of the system not to give special favours remains intact.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Making this change pervasive will truly transform the Public Service delivery to be even better in meeting citizens’ needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To bring about a change in human behaviour, we need to make changes to the system that influences it most, which is the HR system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This brings me to Mr Louis Ng's question.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, during the Budget Debate, Mr Ng expressed concern that there is a culture of compliance, public officers dare not speak up for fear of getting into trouble, and they gave up trying to improve things because such efforts would be in vain and, therefore, some of them say "Let's stop caring".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Louis Ng may not be aware, but the Public Service is undergoing a major transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And it is self-initiated, demonstrating the long-standing ethos of serving with heart and commitment, and always striving to do better for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Head of Civil Service has called on public officers to have a "constructive discontent", of being dissatisfied with the status quo and wanting to do better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have urged the service to be bold – "think big, start small, act fast".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This deep change cannot happen if the Public Service does not welcome ideas from its own officers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As Mr Louis Ng has acknowledged, many Permanent Secretaries and Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) engage staff directly to hear them out.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I agree with him that there ought to be across-the-board practice.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, all agencies today conduct regular employee engagement surveys, and many carry out other organisational development initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Notwithstanding all these efforts, like all big and complex organisations, when there is change, there will be those driving it, those supporting it, those worried about it, those wanting change in a totally different direction and some resisting it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are determined to succeed in this exercise and overcome the challenges and obstacles.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Kok Heng Leun quoted me on this in their speeches during the Budget Debate and I thank them for that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the next question is: if you accept that the biggest obstacle is ourselves, the next question is: who does "ourselves" refer to?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And the answer really is: it starts with me.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, for me as the Minister, I constantly have to ask myself: am I giving policy directions that are bold enough, clear enough and empowering enough for my staff?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For a Permanent Secretary or CEO, he will ask if he has built an effective organisation with the forward-looking culture that can embrace change.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For a Director, he will ask if, within his area of responsibility, he has sufficiently made improvements, made Public Service more effective, service the public better and empowered, motivated and rallied his troops, the people reporting to him.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And for an individual officer, he will ask whether he has acquired the skills to do the job better and serve the public better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If the starting point is that everyone else is an obstacle except yourself, then I say you need to care more about doing your work and doing your part, recognising that there are pros and cons to every proposed change, and that effecting change involves patience, persistence and a hard slog.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Louis Ng, although he is not a Public Service officer, as an MP and a public figure, he can do his part, too.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If some civil servants tell you they dare not speak up, you can assure them that, from your own experience, you have always spoken up and never got into trouble.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If they feel the system does not allow them to make a difference, ask them what it is that they want to change.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If it is a philosophical shift in Government policy, like selling land to pay for healthcare costs, then you have to explain to them this is not the policy of this current Government.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Where the Public Service has fallen short, it will address the problem.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when generalisations that tar the entire service with the same brush are made in public and, worse, further spread through media, it does not do justice to our officers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I say to Mr Louis Ng, be part of the change, work with and encourage the Public Service as it strives to transform itself to build a better future for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Assoc Prof Dr Muhd Faishal Ibrahim, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Patrick Tay asked a very pertinent question how the Public Service can look beyond paper qualifications, to recognise skills and competencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I believe Dr Teo Ho Pin asked that question, too.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This has important relevance to the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We want to encourage Singaporeans to uncover their passions and aptitudes in a diverse range of skills and master them through lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We want a meritocracy of deep skills, not one of past academic results.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But what I think the Public Service can continue to improve on is the recruitment criteria, how schemes are structured and how people are placed into the schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For certain schemes, where officers have to analyse data, develop policies or even help lead large complex organisations, we do need to look out for applicants with cognitive skills, and academic results is one proxy to measure that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, for work that is vocational or skills-based in nature, and there are plenty in the Public Service, there is much less need to sort or select based on academic results, or structure diploma and degree holders into different schemes with different salary scales and structures.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And beyond the point of recruitment, it is on-the-job performance that determines the officer's progression.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we do not do this, we can have a situation where someone without a degree but has mastered the craft after many years of experience and on-the-job training is pegged below a fresh degree graduate doing the same job.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This does not do justice to mastery and craftsmanship.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: PSD has done this merger for the generic Management Executive Scheme in the Civil Service in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And as Assoc Prof Dr Muhd Faishal mentioned, MOE has also done this, so diploma and degree graduates now all come under the same Education Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One most recent example is the Air Traffic Control Officer (ATCO) scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Changi Airport is one of the busiest airports in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To keep our skies safe and secure, we need highly skilled and competent Air Traffic Controllers (ATCOs) to plan, guide and direct air traffic in and out of Changi Airport.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) prepares ATCOs for the job through a very rigorous skills-based training programme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: PSD will work with other public agencies to identify other areas and other schemes where we can implement this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are, however, situations where the profession or the industry feels that a separation of schemes between diploma and degrees is necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In those cases, we will establish a clear, performance-based pathway for an officer to upgrade from the diploma scheme to the degree scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is what the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) will do for the Social Work profession.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, certified social workers need to be social work degree holders.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As such, those who hold relevant diplomas, for example, the Social Work diploma from Nanyang Polytechnic, can enter the sector as social work associates (SWAs), playing a supporting role to the degree holding social workers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To enable more diploma holders to become social workers, MSF has endorsed a new pathway.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Through this programme, diploma graduates and promising SWAs with work experience will be able to undergo social work training with suitable employers, while attending classes at SUSS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a work-learn pathway, recognising that social work is really a craft and is skills-based in nature.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the end of the three-year programme, the trainees will attain a Bachelor of Social Work and be certified a social worker.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Minister Desmond Lee will speak more about this at the COS for MSF.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, I will conclude by talking about an agency that has been making a successful leap in changing its mindset and operating model.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One public agency that is really this is the National Parks Board (NParks).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Its vision has evolved over the years from creating a Garden City to having a City in a Garden.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This reimagining of its mission led to innovative projects that integrated nature with our urban landscape, such as Gardens by the Bay, a garden built on prime, reclaimed land, for an extended Central Business District (CBD), which is now a popular destination for locals and a must-see for tourists.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is also the Botanic Gardens, a national park within the city centre, now a United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site and a source of pride for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In my dealings with NParks, I found that they put citizens' interests at the centre of whatever they do.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: NParks also uses technology to help officers work better and more productively.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: NParks' people are valued for their skills and passion in this field.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All officers are hired into the same Management Executive Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our City in a Garden is the best place for these officers to polish their craft.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Public Service never leads in terms of remuneration and benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We see what the industries are offering and try our best to be competitive so that we have our fair share of talent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But where it concerns defining our missions, adopting of new technologies or HR practices in response to emerging opportunities or national challenges, we must be prepared to be pioneer implementers and make that demonstrative impact.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is our role in Singapore's transformation journey, to continuously improve our service to the public and build a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, what measures does the Government have to review our population strategies so that we will have a vibrant economy and a cohesive society?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For a cohesive society, it is necessary to have the majority of residents who are Singaporeans at birth, growing up with common life experiences to facilitate a stronger national identity and a sense of unity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry share with the House its plan to reboot our population growth strategies and policies?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is a beautiful saying, "having a child is like having a little piece of your heart running outside you".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My wife and I are expecting our first born in the coming days.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I find myself wondering aloud: what kind of Singapore will my child grow up in?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Will Singapore still remain open, an exciting land of possibilities?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Or will we become an insular country laden by debts arising from an ageing population?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What are the consequences for the future generations if our current demographics and immigration trends continue?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What are the tradeoffs that we need to make in the next 10 to 15 years?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will we still be able to maintain our low tax rate and high level of benefits to citizens at the same time?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond our current strategy of strengthening the Singapore Core, plugging infrastructure gaps, strengthening integration, improving productivity, and ensuring quality immigration, what other immediate steps must we take now, so that our people support a Singapore that remains open to the world?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Unfortunately, Singaporeans have not been very productive in this respect, myself included.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As a successful and economically vibrant city, we remain an attractive place for foreigners.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What is the Government’s current approach on managing foreign worker inflows so that we can ensure our businesses remain competitive?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: At the same time, what is our approach to ensure that we also assuage the concerns of Singaporeans that these foreign workers may take away rather than add to employment opportunities for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, on the contrary, my wife and I were blessed to welcome our third new addition to our family in December.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, apart from sleep deprivation that has once again visited upon my house, longer nights, messier clothes and a much rowdier house, I must say, with all honesty, that having our three boys has made our love stronger and our home happier, our troubles forgotten and our future so much more worth living and fighting for.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, congratulations are in order to Mr Henry Kwek Hian Chuan in advance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Indeed, parenthood is not just a diaper-changing experience, it is a life-changing one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You learn how sacred and special it is to have given life, to have in your responsibility the care of a new life that is not just a part of your life but quite literally part of you.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yes, admittedly your life changes, it is no longer yours alone as your vocation becomes one of a steward of a precious life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That said, this is not one of those Uniquely Singapore problems.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: TFR has been in decline worldwide for the last 50 years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The question is, has joy gone out from parenthood?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Or is there just too much pressure in society?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we look at the Department of Statistics numbers, it is clear that a larger cohort of young Singaporeans will be entering their peak marriage and childbearing ages in the next decade.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The question that some would definitely ask will centre around what further support or money will the Government be able to provide to encourage Singaporeans to marry earlier and to help build stronger families for Singapore's continued survival.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Government has provided lots of practical assistance which I do not have to repeat.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With all the grants and support extended to young Singaporeans, this ought to be the best time to have children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I think what is glaring in the conversation, not just in Singapore, but in many other countries facing low TFR, is just how overtly nationalistic and wider societal demands there are to justify families having more children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Russia, they launched a "Give Birth to a Patriot" scheme and Taiwan politicians refer to the low TFR as a "threat to national security".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
