text: Even in Denmark, a government-sponsored advertising campaign went even further by simply asking Danes to, forgive me if I pronounce this wrongly, "Knald for Danmark", which I will not attempt to translate for fear of the hon Speaker's censure.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The country's survival, economic growth, national duty, patriotic mission – all big words.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Important but missing in all of these campaigns is, most important of which, the love that parenthood truly brings, the importance of marriage, the joy of family life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we encourage fruitful marriages without relying on focus on national needs?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we emphasise the joy of family without the need to refer to tax burdens and incentives?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Those are perhaps more critical questions for us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we, therefore, support young Singaporeans in their very personal parenthood journeys without being too intrusive?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we build a city and a culture that will both value the career aspirations of the young and yet have a strong support network for parenthood and family life?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can we reduce the unequalness of our grants and schemes that segregate mothers between those who are working and those who are not?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This discriminates between both groups who are equally noble in their duties as mothers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can we do more for adoption and thus perhaps reduce abortion rates?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most of all, apart from the policies we have in place, which are useful nonetheless, how do we let young couples know that despite the sacrifices involved in parenthood, our society, our country, our Government recognise and support it.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am not sure what the slogan is, but certainly the videos are quite entertaining.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our population is ageing rapidly and we are not having enough babies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the years, the Government has rolled out many Baby Bonuses and incentives to encourage parenthood.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What more can we do to encourage Singaporeans to have more babies?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is one area where the gender gap is skewed more in favour of women than men, so I am quite glad we are making strides for the rights of men.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we can make things fairer for fathers because that would definitely make things fairer for mums as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Centre for Fathers' Chief Executive Peter Quek has said that today's fathers are a lot more hands-on in raising their children and they are the beginnings of a cultural shift and more men actually want to step up to the plate to be more participative caregivers to their kids and also to their elders.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some men are actually even choosing to be full-time caregivers because it comes down to a simple decision between husband and wife about who can drive the car and who cannot, or whose parent is the one who needs care or who has a greater chance at being fast-tracked in their career and who does not.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Full-time male caregivers are particularly courageous because they know what they are doing runs up against the grain of predominant assumptions about gender roles.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Though these men are clear and have no regrets about their choices because they see the impact they are making on their kids and the elders in their care, they still feel hesitant and some even say they feel ashamed about letting other people know what they do for work.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I find this really troubling because they have nothing to be ashamed about and they are doing really noble work with long intergenerational impact and it is the same work that women have been doing for years, by the way.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What can we do to further recognise the gifts that fathers are to their children, and how can we help to affirm that men are just as powerful, impactful and necessary a caregiver to their children as women are?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we can offer a longer quantum of parental leave for parents to share as they wish.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But my fellow Nominated MP, Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, in the tea-room just now, who is a new dad, said, "Eh, why not push for more?" So, okay, on his behalf, why not 16?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Allowing more flexibility of leave to be shared between husband and wife would be really useful for working couples who are in this scenario where the woman has a better-paid job and better career-advancement prospects than her spouse.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If they prefer that she remains in full-time employment while he goes part-time or leave the workforce for a season, then they should be allowed to make that decision rather than be forced into arrangements that are just dictated by gender.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This will help couples feel a lot freer to manage their families and finances as they wish and this will also have an impact on the overall output contribution and productivity of our labour force.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: To reduce disruptions to the labour supply, maybe there can be restrictions placed on how this additional leave is to be taken.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I think the United Kingdom (UK) manages that by saying that leave should be taken in weeks rather than days.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, the same amount of adoption leave that is available to mums should be available to dads.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Or alternatively, a longer quantum of gender-neutral adoption leave can be offered for parents to share as they wish.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I will end my cut with a request.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: When I first became an MP in 2006, I had pushed for paternity leave for six consecutive years of COS.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: So, I was delighted that we finally put this into law.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I have been on the board of the Centre for Fathering longer than I have been an MP.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: To me, the situation is akin to less than half of eligible mothers taking up their maternity leave benefits.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: My questions to the Minister are as follows.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: So, if we know the underlying causes for this low utilisation rate, how are we addressing them?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Even if some dads and mums were to feel that the two-week leave is not much in the grand scheme of things, the fact that so few take it up should lead us to relook this policy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: So, I do not want to force paternity leave down the throats of families which do not want to take it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: However, if the obstacle is something else, something that we can address as a matter of policy, then I think we are in a position and we ought to fix it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They also ensure that our young children receive the appropriate stimulations to promote healthy mental and physical developments, which form the essential foundation for their further learning as they move up the education system and even into adulthood.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To avoid a class divide as early as this, we must all the more ensure that children of low-income families receive quality early childhood education and care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, what more is the Government doing to ensure sufficient provision of affordable and quality preschools and care centres at the infant and childcare stages?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Beyond just having more centres, what other support is the Government offering to encourage families to send their children to preschools?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sun Xueling, can you take the two cuts together?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Like childcare, infant care options weigh heavily on the minds of parents.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am concerned that some well-meaning parameters, such as space-to-infant ratio has overly limited the number of places the centre can provide for infants.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What can the Ministry do to ensure affordable and quality infant care places so that young mothers have real options to put their infants in infant care so that they can go back to the workplace post-maternity leave?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Ministry share where the gaps are since employees are keener on FWAs and employers, based on the survey, are willing to let employees benefit from FWAs?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Ministry has been systematic in promoting FWAs for employees, defining such arrangements as being flexi-time, flexi-place or flexi-load.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am keen to see FWAs are being rolled out on a sustainable basis in society, and that can only happen if both employers and employees see the value in the arrangements.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, on the implementation front, can we consider rolling out FWAs on a sectoral basis?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we work with some queen-bee companies in these selected sectors to get early buy-in?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, can we push the boundary by legislating FWAs for selected industries?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My speech will also contain quite a few number of "F" words, specifically flexible, family and friendly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Progress in digital technology has also been the catalyst for the development of collaborative project management platforms that have reduced the need for employees to be housed in the same physical workspace.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These practices have facilitated the gradual transition of business models from those that focus on office presence and facetime to those that emphasise deliverables.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These initiatives are, indeed, starting to make an impact in helping employees better manage demands from work and family.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite these measures, the 20- and 30-somethings remain concerned about their ability to manage their work and family aspirations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And there are, indeed, those who have come to our shores who end up making Singapore their permanent home.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Government needs to be mindful about managing the socioeconomic impact of immigration on Singaporeans, many of us will agree that immigration certainly leads to a richer and more diverse society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as we go about forging a national identity and building an inclusive Singapore, we need to ask ourselves what can be done to manage this new diversity in our society that has been brought about by immigration?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A Canadian Prime Minister, whose country was rated by a study as the second-best for migrants to live in, once said, and I quote, “Diversity is our strength.” As we move forward, and as our society welcomes its share of new citizens, I hope that the Government can share how it plans to strengthen integration and build social cohesion such that we, as Singaporeans, can also view diversity as one of our strengths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Singapore attracts people from all over the world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They want to work and live here and raise their families here.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have seen many different communities come to Singapore to make it a home, enjoying our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These new communities bring with them their language, culture and these add vibrancy to our cultural landscape.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, it is inevitable that, from time to time, we see some tensions as people learn to appreciate different cultures and ways of life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some may feel uncomfortable with or suspicious of people and communities whom they are not familiar with.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Malay, there is a saying "tak kenal maka tak cinta", which means "you do not know so you do not love".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When you do not know someone, it is easy to attribute faults or make that person a common enemy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On occasion, I hear complaints of lack of friendliness and of noise attributed to the newcomers in our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These may seem like petty issues, but it affects our day-to-day lives.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At a more serious level, the newcomers are seen as taking away all our jobs and breaking our families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to accept that global boundaries have become porous and that Singapore's economy is also dependent on it being open.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some people may be here only for a temporary period.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In any case though, they are part of our big community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For Singapore to do well, the community needs to be cohesive and integrated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There needs to be platforms to encourage interaction and foster understanding.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I understand that there are many efforts in place to integrate the different communities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have been married for about six years before I became pregnant with my baby.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I delivered a baby boy last year when I was already 37 years old.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We do see many people marrying later and having children later in their lives.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many of us get caught up with our careers and may not plan the time for finding a partner and building a family.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It takes effort and time to find the right partner.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And most Singaporeans want to have all things in place before they start a family.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Of course, it is best if we can encourage Singaporeans to get settled down and have children when they are younger.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But the reality is that this may be easier said than done.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: With couples marrying later, more married couples may face difficulties in conceiving or have challenges during pregnancy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.52 pm until 3.15 pm.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their thoughtful questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I am very pleased, of course, to know that several Members are contributing to our TFR – Mr Henry Kwek and his wife, Mr Alex Yam, Mr Desmond Choo recently and Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Louis Ng, not so long ago.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And I do echo the Chairman's exhortation that everyone else who can help, please chip in.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Alex Yam has shared with us what is happening in Russia.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And, as it turns out, they have established the scheme called the Order of Parental Glory and they did so in 2009 because Russia also has severely low rates of birth.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And what happens is that to receive the Order of Parental Glory, you go to the Kremlin and the President presents it to you.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But in order to qualify, you have to have seven children.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, I think if we can get there, I am sure something can be arranged at the Istana.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At last year's COS debate, I focused on how we can support Singaporeans to marry and raise a family.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is a delicate balancing act to meet all three objectives.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is also about sensitivity towards how connected people feel with our evolving society.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Henry Kwek asked about the Government's strategies to secure a bright future for Singaporeans in view of our demographic challenges.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this debate, I will provide an update on our population strategies and outlook, how we are planning ahead, as well as further measures to support marriage and parenthood.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, we have three broad strategies to shape a healthy population profile.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, to enable all Singaporeans to age with purpose and grace.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, to make Singapore a Great Place for Families where marriage and parenthood are achievable, enjoyable and celebrated.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And third, to maintain a careful balance in our foreign worker as well as immigrant flows.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members will recall that the debate reaffirmed that "seniors are a gift to society", and we need a "whole-of-Singapore effort" to build a "nation for all ages".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our ambition is to enable all Singaporeans to age confidently with purpose, grace and dignity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many who wish to continue working past the legal retirement age of 62 have been able to do so with our re-employment policies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is the fifth highest employment rate when compared against the 35 Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By 2020, this proportion is expected to increase to seven in 10.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But as Senior Minister of State Dr Amy Khor shared last month, we must continue to deepen our efforts at three levels: at the individual level, to enable seniors to continue pursuing their passion or causes, to work as long as they wish to; at the family level, to empower caregivers to give better support to our seniors to age-in-place; and at the community level, to build stronger communities of care, to complement family support for seniors.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also want our seniors to stay healthy as they live longer.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With good health, more seniors who wish to work can do so.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That is why we raised the re-employment age from 65 to 67 last year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also provide employers wage offsets through the Special Employment Credit to encourage them to employ seniors.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, under the Adapt and Grow initiative, we enhanced support for mature professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMET) jobseekers, to make it more compelling for employers to hire them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also recognise that with extended longevity, families worry about their ability to manage should serious disability strike.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why, having introduced MediShield Life, MOH is reviewing ElderShield to strengthen support for seniors requiring long-term care.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue supporting Singaporeans to lead active lives well into their silver years, contributing to the economy and society while enjoying strong bonds with their families and communities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, we should find meaningful ways to support families who are bringing up the next generation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why our second broad strategy to shape a healthy population profile is to make Singapore a Great Place for Families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This means strongly supporting Singaporeans' aspirations to marry and have children so that both are achievable, enjoyable and celebrated.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singaporeans continue to value families, and the pace of family formation remains strong.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the last four years, the number of citizen marriages and births has been above the past decade's average.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But as Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Gan Thiam Poh highlighted, our TFR has remained low.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It has hovered at around 1.2 in recent years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Why this apparent contradiction, when the number of births has been higher in the past few years?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This chart shows our citizen population by five-year age groups.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: From the 1950s to mid-1960s, we experienced a "Baby Boom", where births reached elevated levels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These cohorts are now in their mid 50s to 60s.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When many of these "Baby Boomers" married and started having children, we saw an echo effect in the late 1980s and 1990s where births also reached elevated levels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are the cohorts which Mr Alex Yam spoke about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, many of these "echo Baby Boomers" would be about 20 to 30 years old.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are included in the denominator used for calculating TFR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But they are only just entering the peak child-bearing ages.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Compared to earlier cohorts, more of them are not yet married or have not started having children.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When they do, we can expect the numerator, which is the number of births, to increase further.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Like Mr Melvin Yong, Members may wonder if our TFR will further decline, as parenthood competes with other priorities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Or could this dip be more like that of the year 2010, where it appeared to have been due to couples holding back parenthood plans in 2009 because of the Global Financial Crisis?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But based on many interactions with young people, I remain convinced and optimistic that we should continue to strengthen support for young families.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Consistent with my own observations, our surveys show that a large majority of young Singaporeans want to marry and have children.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, what is also very clear is that these are not their only life goals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Half of the singles aged 21-35 whom we surveyed in 2016 wanted to focus on their career or studies before marrying.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Almost eight in 10 said that travelling was an important life goal.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One couple who managed to start a family, while pursuing their interests, are Kenny and Peiru.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are a sporty and adventurous couple who enjoy travelling and exploring the outdoors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As they were about to get their keys to a new Build-To-Order (BTO) flat in Punggol Waterway, they planned for their wedding.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They knew that they wanted a meaningful occasion with family and friends and decided this was achievable without over-spending.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Soon after getting married, Peiru found that she was expecting, and the couple put their sports and travel plans on hold.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, as soon as Peiru was out of confinement, they resumed their active lifestyle but, this time, with a new focus – making sure that baby Faith is part of it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, they recently took Faith on a family-friendly coastal hike in Perth, slightly less challenging than what Kenny and Peiru are used to, but it is a start.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Just like Kenny and Peiru, young Singaporeans today have many opportunities to pursue their passions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They may also prefer having their own home or establishing themselves financially before settling down.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These factors have contributed to Singaporeans marrying and having children later.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For some couples, it is not that they set out to marry late.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government cannot interfere with how people go about finding a partner, or whether and when they start trying to have children.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we can help those who are ready to settle down.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Alex Yam spoke about the Government's support for Singaporeans to marry and have children earlier, and we thank him for his suggestions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We recently strengthened support, especially for young Singaporeans, in three main areas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission to distribute a compilation of the Government's key support for marriage and parenthood?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, we helped more couples get a home of their own more quickly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The vast majority of couples like Kenny and Peiru that applied for a BTO flat in a non-mature estate were able to select a flat by their second try, and all were able to do so by their third try.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, we enhanced preschool support to give parents greater peace of mind that their children are well taken care of while they work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sun Xueling and Ms Tin Pei Ling had asked whether we can do more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government is committed to ensuring that every parent who wants a preschool place for their child will be able to have one.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Over the past five years, we increased preschool capacity by 50%.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are now about 7,800 infant care places and 140,000 childcare places.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also ramped up affordable, quality places through the Anchor Operators (AOPs), Partner Operators (POPs) and MOE Kindergartens, with a focus on new estates with many young families.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, a median-income family who enrols their child in an AOP pays about $350 a month for full-day childcare, after Government subsidies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) will continue to increase provision of affordable and quality infant care and childcare places.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, we will continue to safeguard the safety and well-being of children in preschools, including through regulation on space norms, which Ms Sun Xueling asked about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MSF will elaborate more on ECDA's preschool efforts later in the COS debate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Darryl David and Ms Sun Xueling asked about the progress made in encouraging more family-friendly workplaces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have, indeed, strengthened work-life support to help working parents achieve both career and family aspirations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, a working couple can access 20 weeks of paid leave and two weeks of unpaid leave in their child's first year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin suggested increasing leave support for fathers and extending adoption leave to adoptive fathers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, adoptive fathers already enjoy the same Paternity and Shared Parental leave provisions as biological fathers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also progressively enhanced our leave provisions for fathers over the years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For instance, we introduced Paternity Leave in 2013 and doubled it to two weeks in 2017.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Similarly, we increased Shared Parental Leave from one to four weeks over the same period.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In total, fathers, including adoptive fathers, can tap on up to eight weeks of leave to care for their children in the first year of birth.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our unions know that each time parenthood-related leave is enhanced, there is some risk of inadvertently denting the employment prospects of parents and causing some friction with other employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Given the recent enhancements to the legislated leave provisions, we will give businesses some time to adjust.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the meantime, the Public Sector is piloting an additional four weeks of unpaid infant-care leave, for both fathers and mothers, to test the general viability of longer parental leave.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is only six months since we implemented that pilot.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have got more than 80 staff who have taken it up.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is still a bit too early to form a view.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I think the feedback from these staff who have taken the extended leave is that the leave has been very helpful.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also continue to encourage more fathers to make use of the enhanced leave provisions to care for their children.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Mr Seah Kian Peng pointed out, there is still room for improvement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government pays for the Paternity Leave in full and we hope it helps employers to be supportive of employees who are new fathers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition to parental leave, we have strengthened support for workplace flexibility.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More than 350 employers, covering about 250,000 employees, have adopted the Tripartite Standard on FWAs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was launched just about six months ago.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Three in four of these employers are from the private sector, including small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I believe Ms Sun Xueling will agree that this is a good first step, as a society, in moving towards encouraging FWAs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will encourage more employers to sign on to this Standard to distinguish themselves as employers with progressive workplace practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will speak more on the issue of FWAs during the COS debate for the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the same time, these support measures would not work if employees do not have the confidence to tap on them because of unsupportive supervisors or co-workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why the Government takes a multi-pronged approach to helping Singaporeans achieve their marriage and parenthood aspirations, including by encouraging employers and community organisations to lend strong support.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will continue to enhance our policies where possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, we will do more to help couples own a home faster.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As announced by Minister Heng Swee Keat last week, we have enhanced the Proximity Housing Grant to provide more support for couples who wish to live together with or near their parents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some young couples are ready to settle down earlier in life and wish to apply for a BTO flat.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will provide more flexibility in our grant and loan processes to better support them in owning a home.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister Lawrence Wong will share more later in the debate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, we will provide more assistance for couples who face difficulties conceiving.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is also what Ms Rahayu Mahzam suggested.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, we will enhance healthcare assurance for young families.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOH will share more details in the coming months.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While we have significantly enhanced parenthood-related leave provisions, there are sometimes unexpected caregiving needs that put families under stress, for example, congenital conditions or sudden illnesses among infants, or in cases of multiple or pre-term births.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To promote voluntary adoption by employers, such leave will be unpaid and kept to four weeks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Standard also provides up to two weeks of unpaid leave for employees with immediate family members who are hospitalised.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, this Tripartite Standard will really help the sandwich class, that is, those who have to look after the young as well as the seniors in their homes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The fifth enhancement is to extend and enhance the Work-Life Grant.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will provide more support to businesses to encourage the adoption of FWAs, in particular, job sharing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These will make it easier for employers to implement practices that enhance family-friendliness.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will share more in a few days.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides these policy enhancements, employers, co-workers and the community can also provide strong support.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, Mr Alex Yam will be glad to know that the PA's Embracing PArenthood Movement, which celebrates young families, reached out to 30,000 parents and caregivers across 250 celebrations held nationwide last year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I have attended some of these very joyous occasions that signal to the new parents that you are not alone and that the whole community is here to support.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And so, through this Movement, several parent support networks have also been formed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will continue to strongly support Singaporeans to start families sooner rather than later.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Making Singapore a Great Place for Families is a continuous effort.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government will do its part and work with employers and community organisations to keep up the momentum.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Henry Kwek asked about our foreign workforce and immigration policies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our third strategy to achieve a healthy population profile is to maintain a careful balance in foreign worker as well as immigrant flows.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Growth was 1% per year over the last five years, compared to 3% per year for the previous five years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to show one slide and this has got to do with our working-age citizen population.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even with immigrants, the number of Singaporeans aged 20 to 64 is projected to peak at 2.2 million around 2020 and then it will decline thereafter.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Without immigration, it would have started to shrink earlier and decline at a much faster rate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Recognising this trend, we have started transforming our economy towards lower manpower reliance and more productivity-driven growth.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Minister for Finance shared last week, last year's productivity growth was the highest since 2010.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We should press on to raise productivity in all sectors of our economy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, to sustain a healthy growth momentum that provides good jobs for Singaporeans, some workforce growth is still necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, we will continue to support higher labour force participation among locals and balance these efforts with a calibrated flow of foreign workers that complements our local workforce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: From 2013 to 2015, foreign employment grew but at a much slower pace than the earlier years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, since 2016, due mainly to cyclical factors in the Construction and Marine and Offshore Engineering sectors, foreign employment fell even as local employment expanded.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM has also stepped up efforts to emphasise complementarity between the local and foreign workforce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Fair Consideration Framework (FCF) sets out clear expectations for companies to practise fair hiring.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Human Capital Partnership Programme supports progressive employers who are committed to strengthening local-foreign complementarity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A new Capability Transfer Programme will support businesses, associations and professional bodies for the specific purpose of building up local capabilities through the help of foreign expertise.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By focusing on local-foreign workforce complementarity, we continue to see good employment outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Employment rates for those aged 25 to 64 are on an upward trend.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And over the last five years from 2012 to 2017, real income at the median and 20th percentile of full-time employed citizens grew by 3.9% and 4.3% per annum.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, we can better match local jobseekers to occupations with significant vacancies and help them access new jobs that are being created.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will benefit both businesses and the local workforce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM will provide a fuller update later in the debate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is significantly less than in the past.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: From 2010-2020, we are looking at 1% to 2% growth.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Compared to the previous decades, you will see very clearly that workforce growth will slow significantly in this decade.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Having said that, we think that it is a more sustainable pace going forward.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We appreciate businesses' efforts to make adjustments, and the economic agencies will continue providing strong support through various schemes and programmes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While managing foreign workforce flows to complement the local workforce, it is also important that we carefully manage immigration flows.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Without immigration, not only will our working age population shrink rapidly, the total number of citizens will eventually decline.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why, each year, we take in a carefully balanced number of new immigrants.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if our immigration policy will change, given our low TFR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If our current citizen population was able to replace itself with a TFR of 2.1, we can have a stable citizen population well into the future.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What you see on the chart is that our citizen population is 3.4 million today, or as of 2017.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And if you project well into the future, assuming a TFR of 2.1, then even without immigration, the citizen population is stable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But, at the current TFR, and if there was no immigration at all, our citizen population will shrink in the long term.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You see that through the blue line which assumes a constant TFR of 1.2 and no immigration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At around the current rates of immigration, we are close to achieving the same effect as if we had full-replacement TFR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The dotted lines, one that shows immigration of about 15,000 Singapore Citizenships granted a year; the other dotted line higher on the graph, 25,000.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, with a moderate level of immigration, we can prevent the citizen population from shrinking in the long term.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also taken in a steady number of Permanent Residents (PRs) each year, many of whom take up citizenship eventually.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But as I said earlier, it is more than just the numbers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are selective about the profile of our immigrants, because it affects how we grow a strong national identity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why we prioritise not only those who can contribute, but those who are also prepared to sink roots in Singapore and can integrate well here.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A significant proportion of citizenships granted each year have family ties with Singaporeans and/or lived here for some time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Kenny, whom I mentioned earlier, was born in Malaysia, and he came here to study when he was 18.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are many examples like him and Peiru, where a Singaporean marries a foreigner and both have chosen to settle in Singapore to raise their young ones.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Darryl David and Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked what more can be done to strengthen integration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It starts with how we see ourselves and how our nation was built up.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Prime Minister Lee reminded all of us in his New Year Message, "Our forefathers came from China, India, the region and beyond, leaving their families behind, to seek better lives here.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They came as sojourners, with no intention to stay.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They brought their families over or formed families here.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They built hospitals, schools, mosques, temples and churches for their communities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They brought their own cultures and traditions, interacted with one another, and wove these strands together into a rich and diverse tapestry.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Over time, out of their shared experience grew a Singaporean identity, a shared sense of being rooted in Singapore", end quote.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The journey of integration starts with this understanding and is deepened though relationships, which have to go both ways.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, one in three marriages are between a Singaporean and non-Singaporean.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Just as Peiru's family opened their hearts and welcomed Kenny into their lives, so, too, can Singapore continue to welcome people who are able to contribute, and certainly those who are committed to sinking roots here.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And in the same way that Kenny has won over Peiru's family through his words and deeds, Singaporeans hope that newcomers can adapt to our local cultures and social norms and, for immigrants especially, to fully embrace our way of life.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To facilitate this process, the National Integration Council works with its partners in the community, workplaces and schools to help newcomers settle in better and appreciate Singaporean values and way of life.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These projects encourage immigrants and locals to bond over various interests, such as sports and volunteerism.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Companies and schools have also stepped up to organise events on their own.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Integration will always be a work-in-progress and take time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Ms Rahayu Mahzam correctly points out that while we seek to preserve the character of our society, we must also maintain a sense of openness to those joining us.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This duality must firmly remain embedded in our DNA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is the foundation on which we can build a harmonious, multiracial and multicultural society that stands the test of time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I have outlined our approach for achieving a healthy population profile.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are also investing in building up quality infrastructure.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The size of our population will be an important input for planning.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The respective Ministers will update on the progress of the plans under their charge.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, to conclude, we have planned ahead to address our long-term challenges of an ageing population and low TFR, to ensure a healthy population profile that improves the lives of each generation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are well prepared for the future and have a strong foundation upon which to keep building up a nation that we will always be proud to call home.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: I noted that the Minister mentioned that the immigration rates more or less will be stable.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: But can that rate be sustained, because all these new immigrants will one day become old?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: They will be part of our ageing population.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Does the Minister want to give a quick response?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I agree and I hear the Member's question.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will certainly respond to him later during clarification time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Smart Nation has since evolved with the national agenda and I believe that Smart Nation needs to be inclusive to all and I would like to make special mention for the inclusion of seniors to enable better ageing, those with special needs and the vulnerable in the community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It would be great if Smart Nation can leverage on assistive technologies and even AI, which may be able to augment the capabilities of our seniors and enhance their employability in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should also make use of health telepresence, sensors and smart logistics to reduce the need of our seniors and caregivers to make visits for checkups and collecting medication.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Technology has the potential to also help bridge greater collaboration between patients, caregivers and medical care.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On that note, I would like to ask how we can better involve seniors in our Smart Nation initiatives so that they can also feel and identify with its intended benefits.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With an ageing population, this segment will become one of our largest user segments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For those with special needs, I would like to ask whether there are plans to study how we can make it easier for them to be economically active, better cared for and more mobile?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is Smart Nation’s agenda for our special needs community?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does PMO have concrete goals and specific timelines on its push towards Government digitalisation and what are its plans to ensure that the digital rollout is on course?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As an advocate of Smart Nation, I hope to see how our Government’s digitalisation efforts can help the vulnerable better.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the Public Sector (Governance) Act in place, we should aim to use technology to speed up approvals for social assistance and other schemes that can help the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have seen many low-income families or elderly get caught in the process because of lack of documentation or access to information, especially in complicated family situations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, we should also develop smart systems that can empower frontline Government officers to make quicker assessments to approve help schemes and cut through the bureaucracy of approvals more quickly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should leverage the Government’s vast sources of touchpoints and data across agencies to provide the frontline officers with a more holistic view of cases, to make quicker and better decisions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Smart Nation, if done well, Mr Chairman, will be a gamechanger for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, for that to happen, Singaporeans must understand it, feel its impact and stand to benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, our Smart Nation initiatives (SNI) have been launched in earnest and it is pervading across almost all sectors of our society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: SNI is about harnessing the full power and potential of digital and smart technologies to create a whole new dimension in jobs and business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also have the impression that SNI is also about planning strategically about our future technology infrastructural needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have seen how, today, we are able to get many things done without even moving out of our seats in the office or at home.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But there are areas we need to look into.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Allow me to share one example where a doctor remarked that he finds there is just too much to pick up − he shared with me − and navigating the digital maze is just too onerous.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The thought that crossed my mind was, if a professional finds it difficult, then what about the elderly in our community, especially those with low literacy?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, we read of disruptions in the digital age.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The spread of viruses, hacking, theft from bank accounts, and the occasional technical glitches.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mailboxes are bombarded by spam mails that flood the mailbox purportedly from Government Ministries and even the Singapore telecom companies (telcos).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singtel subscribers shared with me almost daily that they get such mails and even the anti-virus could not stop these spams.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can telcos and banks, whose services are widely used by individuals and businesses, act against phishing and spams?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite all these, we cannot stop moving ahead in digital technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In essence, what is our Smart Nation narrative at this juncture?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, at the core of Singapore’s Smart Nation vision is how digital technologies are leveraged to improve the lives of our citizens and enable our businesses to innovate to meet the aspirations of our people.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how is the Government making digital services more citizen-centric and providing anticipatory services?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Technological disruption and digitalisation are bringing about rapid changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To remain globally and regionally competitive, Singapore has to harness digital technologies and accelerate the transformation of our economy and society.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Have these strategic projects simplified and improved life and work for citizens?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Has digital technology and the digitalisation of businesses driven economic productivity?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the Government plays a strategic role in making Singapore a Smart Nation, one of the goals of SNDGG is to lead the development of the Smart Nation in partnership with the public, private and people sectors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister share the progress of the engagement and partnership of SNDGG with the private and people sectors?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Has there been progress of public support for technology adoption and what more can be done to accelerate it?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the Budget places a premium on the role of our SNIs.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When I was reading for my Masters at Stanford University more than a decade ago, I was inspired and over-awed by the entire experience but, in particular, nothing impressed me more than a module in law, science and technology.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: At that time, it was just a module.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Ten years later, it is the entire Masters focus group altogether.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That focus group or cluster combines the resources of renowned Stanford faculty experts, alumni practising on the cutting-edge of Technology Law, technologically-savvy students from the United States (US) and beyond, and it is located in the heart of the Silicon Valley – the inspiration for Smart Nation and Smart Technology.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As we learnt, when we were debating on the rise of fake news and the responses that this House should take in time through the Select Committee's report, we noticed that there can be a "dark side" to tech.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: For fake news, we know we have to find ways to prevent, detect and combat it.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: You can patch news software, but you cannot patch reputation when it has been harmed.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Just as fake news can be damaging to reputation, big data and AI can perhaps be more damaging.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The potential for harm resulting from big data is all around us.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is embedded in the network services that we use daily.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is used in our smartphones, smart cars, global positioning system (GPS), even washing machines, and it is controlled with respect to and could be deployed by a coterie of very powerful companies.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Smart Nation strategic national projects are set to use these big datasets.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I say "mindful" because every time we download a new app, we agree to the "terms and conditions", but how many of us actually appreciate every line when we tick that box?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, complex questions have arisen and will continue to arise.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Who derives the benefits from this aggregate data?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What harm is done to individuals who have their data mixed with other persons', without any concern for maintaining identifiable, anonymised information?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What duty will the Government and these corporations have to protect individuals' privacy and minimise any harm that could arise?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The New York Times very recently raised a specific example, which I would like to share with the House and I think would apply equally in Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They suggested that the medical profession has, as a core ethic, the statement: first, do no harm.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Silicon Valley tech entrepreneurs have a different mantra, Mr Chairman.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Theirs is "build it first, ask for forgiveness later".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would not want to change this work ethic partly because that is where innovation is born.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But having said that, how do we square these diametrically opposed ethos?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What happens then when you combine both these worlds – public health and Silicon Valley – when medical big datasets are crunched, processed and unthinkingly analysed by certain programmers for private benefit?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The choices that get made in building technology also have these social ramifications.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: Would we have a Select Committee, and could we look into doing so?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Chairman, Smart Nation is not merely about technologies but also a transformation in itself, a way of life and a way of conducting businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To be pervasive, we need to tackle barriers to adoption, such as multiple platforms for cashless payment and the lack of manpower, to implement these changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What efforts are in place to integrate SNIs into our ITMs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For Smart Nation to succeed, it must also have sufficient competent manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Ministry can consider also tapping on converting mid-career talent by adapting the Professional Conversion Programmes (PCP) for public sector needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are after all good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The desired scale of the Smart Nation movement requires that info-communications technology (ICT) officers in other parts of the Government are also trained and equipped to take on the new initiatives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Will sufficient training be put in place to ensure alignment and scalability?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Accelerating the take-up of SNIs might perhaps require greater policy leverage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In a huge economy like China, there are really only two dominant e-payment systems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government or us can consider picking winners or legislating to require interoperability of our e-payment service providers or along the lines of the Cross-Carriage Measure that has been applied to the telcos.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck, you can take the two cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, the Smart Nation project excites and raises a lot of high expectations amongst the businesses and citizens.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, many are still unclear and they all have different expectations of what is to come and what are the outcomes.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Local startups and SMEs hope that the Smart Nation project could provide them with opportunities or even a lifeline for their businesses, and many look at the Smart Nation project as a way to innovate, create and bail out their businesses.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Most of them hope to work with the Government in such projects.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And learning from smart cities like Estonia and Barcelona, many of the local tech companies and industries over there were involved in the projects very early on in the stage.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Smart Nation can become a platform and opportunity for our local businesses to scale their businesses locally and overseas.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we have the aspiration to become an innovation hub, we need to give our local businesses more opportunities to participate in the Smart Nation project.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For individuals, there is a lot of expectation of what is to come, and whether they could catch up.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some of them wonder if this Smart Nation project is just another system to collect data, or just for data collection.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or would it be a very difficult transition, especially for the elderly?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or would this Smart Nation project make them smarter, as some joked?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The private sector needs to be given a chance for projects to participate in the Smart Nation project, and individuals need to adapt and learn.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But the Smart Nation project's success cannot be solely dependent on the Government's efforts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, Smart Nation is more than a buzzword.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It can be a movement across Government and the economy, bringing people and businesses from different walks of life on board, for example, across public and private sectors, inspiring and attracting engineers, coders, user interface designers wanting to transform an industry or even dare to change how the world sees technology, starting in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It also needs to have tangible benefits for the economy and jobs for people from all walks of life beyond just the technology sector.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we need to look, too, at how Smart Nation can empower businesses to grow faster, work smarter, do better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see this in a very small way today, even with today's technology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Online delivery platforms have helped local small food and beverage (F&B) businesses serve customers further away, a broader clientele, a broader customer base with less floor space needed.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But when it is easier to implement cashless transactions, when it is easier to do identity authentication, either with a touch of a fingerprint or recognition of your face, all these basic services, if opened up, can be application programming interfaces (APIs) for businesses and other service providers to build upon throughout the Singapore ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And how can businesses and citizens, people from all walks of life, contribute to the Smart Nation movement in a way that is constructive and empowering?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: E-payments and National Digital Identity (NDI) are key thrusts of our Smart Nation strategy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: These can help citizens enjoy greater convenience and control in how they go about interacting with businesses and the Government in their daily lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How is the Government ensuring that our people, especially our elderly, are digitally ready?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Cash always works and is a powerful substitute that discourages e-payment adoption.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But we cannot do away with this option or else many elderly and micro merchants will suffer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: There are also practical constraints to adopting e-payments for micro-businesses, for example, a lack of precious real estate at their stalls, and they have to operate several machines in order to process a transaction, cash becomes much faster.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Given this, how will the Government work with private players to overcome these practical challenges?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Are we still on track to implement and proliferate e-payment in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But SingPass has been fraught with issues lately.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How will this affect or delay the implementation of NDI?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How will the Government ensure that NDI will be robust and secure enough since citizens use it to access services and potentially sensitive and personal information?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But Smart Nation requires all of the public, private and people sectors to work together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How then is the Government working with the local private sector players in implementing e-payments and NDI, as well as developing use cases or practical applications for them?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Since then, a number of new Government agencies and interagency task forces have been set up to drive our efforts to achieve that vision.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: It would thus be good if the Government could provide an update on the progress of the various strategic national projects mooted under SNI and link this progress to some tangible outcomes related to those projects.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The development of SNI requires a pool of talent with bold vision and strong technical competencies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: We, therefore, need to grow our talent base and groom individuals to possess a strong mastery of information systems science and the application of actionable intelligence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The creation of a talent pipeline takes time and we have to put in place a robust ecosystem that supports the training, development and deployment of these talents.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Could the Government share what specific steps it is taking to ensure that we have sufficient large and diverse talent bases to deliver on the Smart Nation projects and goals?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Chairman, the Government has been encouraging the private sector to embrace digitalisation so as to increase productivity and develop new trajectories of growth.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Similarly, citizens have been encouraged to go cashless and use technology to achieve greater conveniences in daily living.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These efforts are worthy but, without foundational pieces, such as digital platforms and enabling infrastructure, private initiatives may achieve piecemeal success at best or, even worse, run into technical difficulties during implementation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I would thus like to understand how we are progressing in our five strategic national projects which can lay the foundation for which our society can make better use of digital technology.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: What investments would the Government be making to ensure the running of reliable, resilient and secure systems?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Chairman, we need a concerted and sustained effort to conceptualise, build and manage Smart Nation-related projects.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We should embark on Smart Nation as a new nation-building project.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: What that means is that we need a whole-of-Government approach, an all-talent-on-board drive.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have been hiring ICT professionals piecemeal from the private sector.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Given the enormity and strategic importance of Smart Nation to Singapore, I suspect that we also need ICT talents who understand where we are and the legacy issues we may have and where we hope to get to.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is a Singaporean Smart Nation vision that we want to get to, one that is inclusive and beneficial to all in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As such, how can we grow ICT leaders within the public sector with experience to drive and manage our Smart Nation ambitions?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Elections Department (ELD) said it will pilot a system that will scan the barcode on a voter's identity card to shorten the waiting time for voters at polling stations.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As I understood from the news, the electronic system is only for registration.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Voting will still be conducted using paper ballots with a pen.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Under section 42 of the Parliamentary Elections Act, which describes the manner of voting, subsection (2A)(b) states that "the number, name and description of the voter, as stated in the copy of the register of electors, shall be called out".

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: With the proposed e-registration, the need to call out the voter's particulars would no longer be necessary.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This archaic practice of calling out the voter's particulars, directed at the polling agents, makes sense only if the integrity of the registers of electors is in doubt.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: After contesting in three elections, I have no reason to doubt the accuracy of the registers of electors to require a line-by-line checking by my polling agent on polling day.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The call-out can also be heard clearly in some polling stations due to the acoustics.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Anyone with a mobile phone can secretly record the particulars of the voters as the names and National Registration Identity Card (NRIC) numbers are enunciated slowly.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some People's Action Party (PAP) polling agents would echo the particulars in an even louder voice, which is neither necessary nor provided for under the Elections Act.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, a new process to let registered voters to go to any counter in the polling station to get a ballot paper and to cast the vote into any available ballot box was also proposed last May.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The votes in the ballot boxes will be mixed in the counting stations.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, it makes no sense to require a voter to go to a particular line and to use a particular ballot box at the polling station.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is also about time to replace the antiquated voting booth which was in use for many elections.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The existing booth allows four voters to vote simultaneously but, because of its A-frame design, it does not offer much privacy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is also not very user-friendly for persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: With the proliferation of personal mobility aids of all shapes and sizes, the booth is certainly due for an overhaul.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singaporeans have confidence that so long as CPIB secures evidence of corruption and wrongdoing against a person, it will take action and bring the person to Court to face justice, regardless of his or her background.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The principal tool of CPIB is the PCA which was enacted in 1960.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It has been revised from time to time to ensure that CPIB officers are provided with the legal support necessary for their work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding the latitude of the provision, the primary focus of CPIB was on reigning in corruption in Singapore or corrupt acts outside Singapore which have a detrimental effect within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Recognising that some countries are less adept at handling domestic corruption, the international community has sought to require countries to enact criminal provisions aimed at discouraging legal persons, meaning corporations and natural persons, from engaging in corrupt practices overseas, especially with respect to offering bribes to foreign government officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Both the United Nations (UN) Convention against Corruption, of which Singapore is a signatory, and the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention mandate this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the UK Bribery Act, it is an offence for a UK company not to have taken reasonable steps to prevent the occurrence of bribery overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In light of these developments, I have the following suggestions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, I suggest that the punishment provisions be relooked to ensure that they have a deterrent effect, especially with respect of corporations which cannot be jailed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government, in its reply then, felt there was no need to do so, having regard to the Singapore situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I respectfully suggest that the Government should relook this position, given the international dimension that I have outlined in my speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Presently, anti-corruption policies seem to be something of an afterthought in Singapore Inc.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Disclosure of the existence of an anti-corruption policy by public-listed companies is startlingly low.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does this reflect the general attitude of companies towards anti-corruption policies?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is startling that the existence of bribery contracts and payments somehow seemed to have escaped the notice of Keppel's senior management, board of directors, audit committees and external auditors for 14 years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could this point to the weaknesses in our current company and auditing regime?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Code of Corporate Governance requires, among other things, audit committees to review the policy and arrangements by which persons may raise concerns about possible improprieties and ensure that arrangements are in place for such concerns to be raised and independently investigated and appropriate follow-up action to be taken.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, only listed companies are required to follow the Code of Corporate Governance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All listed companies should set out their appropriate policy on anti-corruption measures and other improprieties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should also review and enhance the requirements for whistleblowing policies in companies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should also consider enhancing the requirements of the independence of the board.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Norwegian company law dictates that where a company has controlling shareholders, the independence of the board is principally intended to protect minority shareholders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, an independent director in our Government-linked company should have no past or present political affiliation to the ruling party or occupational affiliation to the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should also review the PCA to consider if it is sufficiently adequate to fight modern forms of corporate corruption today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not as easy to successfully prosecute corporations, as opposed to individuals, under PCA, due to the way that the legislation is framed.
