speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The OECD Anti-Bribery Convention recommends the establishment of liability of legal persons for the bribery of foreign public officials.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Should we not expressly include the offence of bribery of foreign public officials by both individuals and companies in PCA?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a measure would effectively impose a duty on businesses to enact adequate procedures to prevent persons associated with the business from committing bribery.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Jurisdictions, like Australia, are also considering introducing section 7 type of offences into their own anti-corruption legislation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, we have heard from the previous hon Members about the Keppel Offshore and Marine (O&M) and the SembCorp Marine bribery scandals.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What would we do, going forward, to stop this from happening again?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And even if we cannot avoid the risk altogether, how would we minimise and mitigate that risk?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: To be frank, Mr Chairman, we can ill-afford the reputational damage of a prosecution, deferred or otherwise.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, we have got questions which I would like to pose to PMO.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And these questions are directed at all listed companies and not just Government-linked companies.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: More specifically, is proof provided or are meaningful explanations given that there is an independent element to the board that is able to exercise independent judgement on corporate affairs?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, this applies to listed companies in Singapore on a "comply and explain" basis and is being reviewed to enhance corporate governance standards and practices in Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Could MAS tell the House more about the origins of this review, in light of the question that has been posed, what is MAS' wish going forward?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that they cannot pronounce or take a position because this is an ongoing review, but what led to this review?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And are there certain points that we would like to instill in our corporate culture in Singapore?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the ongoing review of the Code, would MAS comment on whether the burden of maintaining market integrity solely rests on regulators or has it gone beyond this to substantially shift to market participants, such as financial institutions (FIs), as well?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Are FIs, in turn, expected to adhere to rules of responsible business conduct?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Given that publicly listed companies face pressures of quarterly earnings, how does MAS intend to restore ethical responsible business conduct which is particularly relevant to the financial industry?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That is, how would MAS intend to instill a culture that places values above and beyond profits?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They are unique in the field of corporate responsibility, as far as it relates to foreign direct investments.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: While the guidelines are not legally-binding, these recommendations are instructive and persuasive to the 48 governments that abide by them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As a matter of soft law, would MAS consider utilising these guidelines as a benchmark or coming up with guidelines of their own which might be useful, going forward?

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We are in the midst of a digital revolution.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think everyone knows that, and we know that it is transforming our economy, our society, our jobs.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: During the previous industrial revolution, the people and the regions that first got it were the first to adopt the latest technology, achieved a headstart and they made enormous fortunes and amassed great power.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In fact, I often think we are speaking English today because the last industrial revolution began in England and spread to Europe.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The beginning of every new technological shift is often characterised by an initial Gilded Age, an age when there are greater inequality and profits amassed by the few who get it and have access to the new means of production.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It takes time for new skills to be commoditised, the means of value creation to be more widely disseminated, and then you get a larger middle class.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We saw such a golden age in the immediate aftermath of the Second World War, with a demographic dividend, mass education and a massive investment in infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We believe that the current digital revolution reflects such an inflection point.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The pace of change, however, of this revolution will be much faster than the previous industrial revolution.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And that is why we need to ensure that all Singaporeans, and I emphasise all, master the new skills, and that our economy is rapidly restructured.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Then, and only then, will our people have good jobs with good incomes and then we can remain a cohesive and fair society.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So, this is the context, the narrative, behind our Smart Nation efforts.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am glad to inform Mr Zaqy Mohamed, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Teo Ser Luck that we are making good progress.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In particular, we are accelerating the delivery of our Strategic National Projects.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: These form key digital platforms and infrastructure and are essential for a vibrant and innovative digital economy and for us to enhance our Government services.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: These projects are on track and let me quickly give Members some specifics.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, I believe, asked about the progress of the National Digital Identity and of e-payments.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think Members would be aware of the current SingPass system.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It has got two-factor authentication, but that requires you to either have a hard token or to receive a short message service (SMS) message.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The new SingPass mobile app will enable citizens to authenticate ourselves more quickly and conveniently.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It will allow biometric authentication, and Singaporeans who are overseas will not have to wait to receive an SMS probably at some charge before they can log on to SingPass.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The purpose of MyInfo is to eliminate repetitive form-filling and document verification and it will also enhance accuracy.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This will increase convenience, improve service standards and reduce processing time.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I have heard Mr Zaqy Mohamad’s point that maybe we need to take this same methodology to social assistance as well to reduce repetitive form-filling and speed up backroom processes.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Private companies can innovate and build on top of these platforms.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling will be pleased to note that we are enabling businesses, through the MyInfo Developer and Partner Portal, to integrate their own digital services into MyInfo, which is the Government-initiated secure data platform.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Since the portal’s launch in November 2017, just three months ago, more than 150 businesses from various industries have expressed interest in doing so and we look forward to onboarding more later this year.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We are not going cashless for its own sake.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And we are certainly not doing it for tax collection.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The ultimate objective is to lower transaction costs for all businesses and for citizens who are purchasing goods and services.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It is to expand opportunities and, especially for small companies, freelancers, entrepreneurs, the gig economy and the small handicraft maker.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: You want them to be able to access this at the lowest possible transaction cost in order to enhance competitiveness and participation in our economy.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: PayNow was launched by our banks last year to allow easy and immediate funds transfer using the recipient’s NRIC or mobile phone numbers.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: So far, it has been used mostly for mainly peer-to-peer (P2P) payments, between persons, and more than $370 million has been sent on this basis through the PayNow system.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Our public agencies will shortly start using PayNow as well.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In March this year, CPF Board will allow eligible CPF members over 55 to receive their lump sum withdrawal through PayNow.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It means the funds will be transferred within the same day, hopefully on their birthday, rather than waiting five days, which is the current turnaround time.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We will also be piloting the use of PayNow to disburse Edusave Award monies to Institute of Technical Education (ITE) and polytechnic students.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: They will be able to use PayNow in order to pay other businesses and also receive payment from consumers.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This will increase consumer convenience but, more important than that, it will also enable cheaper and infrastructure-light payments systems, which will benefit especially smaller businesses.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I am also glad that the Network for Electronic Transfers (NETS) and EZ-Link are working together to enable the EZ-Link card acceptance at NETS terminals and vice versa.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But we welcome and encourage, and, in fact, we want to make it a rule from now on, to achieve interoperability of wallets and payments systems.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This will make it much more convenient for consumers and businesses.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Another Strategic National Project is the Smart Nation Sensor Platform.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This aims to put in place an integrated nationwide sensor platform to improve municipal services, city-level operations, planning and security.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: You may not feel the direct impact of this straightaway, but a better and more systematic use of sensors and data will enable us to build and run a smarter, greener and more liveable city, including more responsive and reliable public transport, better public security and improved urban planning.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The trials for various aspects of the Smart Nation Sensor Platform are ongoing right now.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ms Jessica Tan and I think Mr Cedric Foo quite rightly emphasised that digital services should be citizen-centric and anticipatory.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Moments of Life initiative is one example where we are reorganising Government services to provide personalised, customised services at a citizen-centric level.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: You used to have to navigate your way to access the myriad of services that the Government provided.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Then our next step was to have a "No Wrong Door Policy", meaning it does not matter which door you knocked on, it was supposed to work and bring you to the right place.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Frankly, I think we need to reorganise the Government so that the delivery of our services is organised based on the citizen rather than the agency providing those services.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And this is actually not a question of technology but of re-engineering our processes.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And if we succeed, then the doors should disappear.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We will test this out for families with babies born in public hospitals first and then roll it out further.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And if the concept works, we will look at other "Moments of Life".

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: On Smart Urban Mobility, we are pursuing initiatives to use digital technologies to enhance comfort, convenience and reliability of our public transport systems and support our vision of a car-lite Singapore.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Ministry of Transport (MOT) will convey more later.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Besides ensuring progress in these Strategic National Projects, we also need to get our approach to data sharing and protection and system resilience and cybersecurity right.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Harnessing the power of data will be increasingly critical for the Government, businesses and citizens as well.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Data, in a sense, is the new currency of the digital age.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I share Assistant Prof Mahdev Mohan's concern that increased data sharing and data use have to be done in an environment where personal data and privacy are robustly protected.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Hence, we have the Public Sector Governance Act which takes effect in April.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It outlines a set of data-sharing practices for the Government, including using only non-identifiable information for policymaking and planning.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Individual officers will be held accountable for safeguarding the information, and the Government will appoint trusted data custodians who will have central oversight over the anonymisation of datasets before they are shared across agencies.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: This clarity is to encourage safe data-sharing in order to enhance policymaking and improve service delivery, and to do so securely.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Assistant Prof Mahdev Mohan made other points on the social, legal and ethical dimensions of digital technology and we will study these points carefully.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: For the private sector, the Personal Data Protection Commission is conducting ongoing public consultation to ensure that the laws of personal data protection remain relevant.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We must also build our Smart Nation on a reliable and secure foundation.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Many Members have highlighted this – Ms Sun Xueling, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ms Sun and Ms Tin referred to the recent SingPass episode.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Basically, what happened was that a software bug was introduced when they updated the two-factor authentication system within the SingPass server.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That led to progressive slowness and eventually a crash.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Unfortunately, this bug was in the backup system, too.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: GovTech is currently investigating the incident and will provide a more comprehensive update when it is completed.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: But I take the Members' point that, for essential platform technology, we cannot afford to get it wrong.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We conduct regular and rigorous audits, and any findings are followed upon thoroughly.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: I think the staff in GovTech know that I am quite obsessive and I drill down to details, so I give the engineers a slightly hard time.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We also work with our business associations to promote cybersecurity, because it is not enough for the Government to be secure, but businesses also need to adopt good cyber hygiene and to make that a business priority.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And, of course, we should remember that citizens also have to play their part.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Minister Yaacob Ibrahim will share more details on our national cybersecurity efforts later.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng highlighted the impact on the economy and jobs creation.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We know that automation, robotics, data analytics and additive manufacturing, or 3D printing, will certainly disrupt manufacturing and logistics chains.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: For a place like Singapore, a city, an entrepot, a port and airport, surely, these have profound implications on us.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We risk becoming irrelevant if we do not transform our infrastructure, systems and skills quickly enough.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: To do this, we need to ensure that workers all across the segments, as well as our SMEs, are able to take advantage of digital tools and master new skills.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Minister Yaacob Ibrahim and Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will share more details on our TechSkills Accelerator and SME Go Digital programmes.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: As Ms Jessica Tan, Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Teo Ser Luck and Ms Tin Pei Ling have also highlighted quite rightly, the Government cannot build a Smart Nation alone, and we need to involve citizens and businesses.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: In this spirit, we are opening our national platforms.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ultimately, our National Digital Identity and e-payments systems need to be open for private sector, not only to just log on, but to actually build innovative new services on top of these platforms.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: GovTech will conduct regular industry briefings to share the Government’s strategic ICT plans and the pipeline of projects.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We have a need; you have a capability; you have a service.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: If it works, we use it; we pay you; we feed our own local ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We need to make sure that all our projects are inclusive-by-design.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: After all, if you pick up any modern handphone today, they are multilingual by design.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And I am going to push to make Government services adopt that same inclusive approach.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We will also be raising the standards of Government digital content, basically checking our websites, portals and services to make sure they are state of the art.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Basically, we have a league table, and we assess everyone's website and tell them which ones do not work, which ones are not ready and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Minister Yaacob Ibrahim and Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will further elaborate on the MCI's digital readiness initiatives.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The digital revolution can be either exhilarating or terrifying, or both.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: It all depends on whether we are ready.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That is why we have embarked on Smart Nation.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: That is why we need to do so with a great sense of urgency.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: We need to ensure that there are good jobs and opportunities for all.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: The Government will continue investing in infrastructure, creating open platforms, sharing open data, facilitating skills upgrading and encouraging our businesses to adopt the latest technologies.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: And you have heard the Budget provisions for that.

speaker: Dr Vivian Balakrishnan
text: Ultimately, this has to be done with an even greater sense of urgency as a whole-of-Government, whole-of-society, whole-of-nation effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Chairman, many members have spoken about the unprecedented pace of technological innovation we are experiencing today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Singapore’s Smart Nation effort seeks to seize the opportunities presented by these changes to create jobs and improve the lives of our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Government will lead the way by transforming itself to become even more digital and data-driven.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Digitalisation is also a key component of the Public Sector Transformation efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Today, I would like to explain just a few of the initiatives that will form part of this blueprint, in response to Members' questions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked how the Government is making its digital services more citizen-centric.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In the design and delivery of our services, we have and will continue to drive a user-centric approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If I may just share about two of these services with Members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This portal removes the need for businesses to approach different Government agencies separately for grant applications and avoids the need to repeatedly provide similar information for each grant application.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Instead of an agency-centric approach, this platform has been designed around the needs of businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: During the development process, engagement with businesses and their feedback have resulted in modifications and improvements to the portal, for example, the ability for company information to be automatically extracted from the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) for grant applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The second user-centric service I would like to highlight is at the other end of the development process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It has been launched, tested and has had many modifications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The service I am about to describe is very nascent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are designing it and beginning the journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are trying to develop a Digital Medical Certificate (DMC).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Patients today have to store and submit paper MCs to their employers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The employee has to take the trouble to submit a copy and potentially an extra form.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The business has to process the paper copy and also store records properly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Instead, digital MCs stored securely online can be easily retrieved and shared as instructed by the patient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Apart from convenience, this will also save costs from printing and processing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The design challenge, of course, is to separate the MC from the existing health records, and to make sure that it does not in any way impinge upon the delivery of healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It will take some time to get this design right.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will start testing this concept at one SingHealth clinic in May 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will start a small pilot to monitor the user experience, learn quickly what works, what does not, what is easy and what is more difficult, before expanding to more clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Start small, iterate quickly, have a bigger vision in mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is the approach we intend to apply to other Digital Government projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will allow the Government to be more agile in harnessing technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Not all the projects will succeed, and some may evolve to be quite different from the original concept.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But this is to be expected in the pursuit of innovative solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Sun Xueling had asked for details on the Government's digitalisation efforts to support our Smart Nation vision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Beyond designing services to be more user-centric, we will also design them to be digital end-to-end.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our aim must be for citizens and businesses to be able to interact with paperless Government services from start to finish anytime, anywhere and on any Internet-enabled device.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To achieve this is not a matter of simply putting services online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It requires the re-engineering of Government processes and our digital infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is a significant undertaking and we are committed to making it happen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One example of how we will re-engineer our digital infrastructure is the Government Technology Stack.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Tech Stack adopts the same platform approach used by tech and software giants, such as Google and Amazon, where common software and hardware services are shared across the organisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is a built-in resilience and it allows agencies to quickly develop and improve new digital services in a cost- and manpower-efficient manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: More importantly, citizens and businesses will experience a more consistent and connected user experience across the spectrum of Government services, since they rely on the same infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are still developing the Tech Stack, but some foundational pieces are already in place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One example is the application programming interface (API) Exchange.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: An API is a common “pipeline” which makes it possible for information to flow between different software applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The GovTech API Exchange was used in the MyInfo pilot that was just described, to allow banks to onboard new customers using Government-verified data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Compared to using more traditional development methods which would have taken typically more than a year, this pilot was developed within just four months and at a lower cost.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Sun Xueling, Ms Thanaletchimi, Mr Darryl David and Mr Desmond Choo also asked how we are building digital capabilities and developing talent within the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our vision for digital transformation is only possible if we deepen our existing engineering and digital capabilities, build new capabilities and also attract the best technical talent to the public sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These centres will house multidisciplinary teams of data scientists, software developers and designers who are experts in their respective domains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This Centre of Excellence will provide an in-house pool of technical experts to implement innovative projects within the Government and deal with challenging problems, for example, the design and architecture of IoT infrastructure solutions as part of the Smart Nation Sensor Platform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The team also collaborated with the Municipal Services Office to build the OneService mobile app, providing its expertise in user experience design and software prototyping to create a better way for citizens to give their feedback on municipal issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This approach will also assist in raising the capabilities of officers across the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For example, the Data Science and AI capability centre designs curricula, and partners training providers to help provide public officers the tools to learn about data visualisation and machine learning techniques.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The officers can then more effectively analyse their data for better policy outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Talented and competent professionals are crucial to deepening these public sector capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to recruit Singaporeans who have committed themselves to applying technology for the public good.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If I may, allow me to highlight two such engineers, Mr Chong Rong Hwa and Mr Lim Zui Young.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Rong Hwa is the older of the two, mid-career, and is a Lead Cybersecurity Specialist in the cybersecurity capability centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He previously worked as a Senior Manager in FireEye, a Cybersecurity and Malware Protection company in the US, and currently leads a team of hackers that "red-team" to identify security issues in Government systems before others do, so that we can pre-emptively resolve them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He has had prior experience as a junior officer in the old Infocomm Development Authority (IDA), before going overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He has then had years of experience overseas in the private sector within the cybersecurity industry, and now he is playing a key role in making our digital services not just agile, but also secure and resilient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He came back to Singapore and to the public sector for several reasons, including family considerations, but also the opportunity to have a career development pathway around deeper technical skills, not just management skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is his first job and he was hired immediately after graduation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He is a Development Operations Engineer in the Application Design, Development and Deployment capability centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He earned a Master’s in Information Systems at the Singapore Management University (SMU) and now works on the Hive Agile Testing Solutions (HATS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They have developed an inhouse automated software testing tool, reduced manual testing costs and developed more robust and stable Government digital services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The scholarship will be open to students who have completed their junior college or polytechnic studies and are keen to pursue a full-time infocomm-related degree in either a local or overseas university.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This career pathway for scholarship holders will include working in technology agencies like GovTech, the Cyber Security Agency (CSA) and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I encourage budding technologists with a passion for public service and an eagerness to take on the technical challenges of the digital age to apply for the Smart Nation Scholarship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: More details will be released later this year.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, let me take the cuts on the ELD and CPIB on behalf of the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, may I thank Mr Png Eng Huat for his confidence in the secrecy of our voting processes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I would also like to thank the Member for his support for the ELD's recent innovation for e-registration and the refinements to the layout of our voting booths.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We note the Member's suggestions on the design of the booths and the reading out of the names.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, on the booth design, we will continually refine the booth design with our stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We actually have a new prototype for the Presidential Elections (PE) 2017 and we will continue to refine this as we go along.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On the second issue, I will note the Member's suggestion on the reading out of the names.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: What we do is that we read out the name and the serial number of the voter in the polling station registered.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we thank the Member for all these suggestions and we will take into account all these suggestions in the next review of the Parliamentary Elections Act.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On the issue of CPIB and anti-corruption, let me, first, thank Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong for their various suggestions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: CPIB is acutely aware of the evolving challenges of corruption and we can never be complacent.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must always be vigilant, especially in the current era, where issues straddle beyond our sovereign territory.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singapore is recognised as one of the least corrupt countries in the world today.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The corruption situation in Singapore remains under control.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As we say, low crime does not mean no crime.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This can be seen from the corruption statistics released by CPIB in recent years which show that Singapore has one of the world's lowest incidence of corruption.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Nevertheless, while absolute numbers are low, we note that the majority of the cases come from the private sector.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is why the CPIB recognises that it is important to engage the private and business sectors to enhance their awareness of anti-corruption measures and to share the best practices with them, as suggested by Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will share some recent efforts by CPIB.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Members may also be aware of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 37001, the anti-bribery management system that was launched in October 2016.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is a newly developed international standard to help businesses and companies implement anti-bribery compliance programmes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Supported by the Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING) Singapore, CPIB was the National Convenor and led a national working group comprising representatives from the trade associations, industry bodies and academia to develop the standard.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: CPIB continues to be proactive in engaging the private sector.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It conducts regular prevention talks and also periodically participates in business sector conferences in its anti-corruption efforts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Enhancing anti-corruption measures in companies ultimately requires constructive public-private sector cooperation and partnership.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Companies must realise that they are ultimately responsible for the proper and ethical conduct of their businesses and recognise that they also play a vital role in our national anti-corruption efforts in preventing, detecting and reporting corrupt behaviour.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: PCA is a key instrument in our national anti-corruption framework.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is thus pertinent that PCA is periodically reviewed to ensure that it remains relevant and effective in combating corruption, especially on some of the issues raised by both Members that concern the trans-border issues.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The last substantial review of and amendments to PCA was in 1989.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The amendments then included increasing the maximum fines for several offences under PCA and adding an offence of giving false information.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Since the 1989 review, the landscape and context in which corrupt offenders operate has changed.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The modus operandi of corrupt offenders has evolved and corrupt transactions of a transnational nature have become more prevalent.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our PCA has to remain effective to deal with the many manifestations of corrupt practices and conduct.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In this context, CPIB and the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) have been reviewing PCA.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This exercise involves a careful study of the current PCA to establish areas where amendments, refinements and updates may be necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On behalf of Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam and the Minister in charge of MAS, I would like to respond to the cut filed by Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member for sharing his views.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Maintaining market integrity is an important objective for the regulator.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But there is only so much that supervision and enforcement can do.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Integrity and good corporate governance have to be internalised by market participants and have to be part of a deep and widespread corporate culture.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The responsibility for high ethical standards and sound business practices falls chiefly on the board, the CEO and senior management, as well as leadership at all levels of the organisation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The leaders have to take charge, put in place the structures and practices, and walk the talk.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, good corporate governance is a combination of both effective supervisory efforts and corporate self-discipline and leadership.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is especially important for the financial sector because the stability of our financial system depends critically on the trust and confidence that the public places in our FIs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fortunately, FIs in Singapore have generally acquitted themselves well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There have been occasional lapses and MAS takes them very seriously, working with the FIs concerned to ensure that they address the lapses and put in place measures to minimise recurrence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Notwithstanding, MAS plays an active role to encourage and foster such a corporate culture amongst FIs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, promote a culture of trust and ethical behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has been engaging FIs regularly, such as through dialogues with boards and senior management of FIs, to promote desirable industry conduct, understand their challenges and also facilitate sharing of best practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has also published guidance on good practices observed from our thematic reviews in areas, such as corporate lending and anti-money laundering controls.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will assist FIs in benchmarking their practices against best-in-class industry standards of conduct.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In addition, MAS has collaborated with industry associations to promulgate good market practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One example is the Singapore Foreign Exchange Market Committee Guide to Conduct and Market Practices for Treasury Activities, which is currently undergoing review.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, when we enact new legislation or guidelines, MAS will engage the industry and explain the intent behind the changes and what problems they were intended to solve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That way, we hope FIs will have greater buy-in for the changes and not comply for compliance's sake.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, monitor and assess FIs' culture and conduct.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This, in engineering terms, is like preventive maintenance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is essential because downstream control weaknesses and misconduct can be avoided if signs of weak culture or poor ethics are identified early.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In its inspections and supervisory reviews, MAS does not just review governance policies and control processes but also evaluates if the FI has a supportive culture that incentivises the right behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, during inspections, MAS officers will meet with ground staff to assess if the "echo from the ground" resonates with the "tone from the top", in other words, whether the desired culture and risk appetite determined by the board and senior management have been effectively cascaded throughout the organisation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS also looks for potential red flags, such as whether risk and control functions have sufficient stature and whether incentive structures bring about responsible risk-taking and ethical conduct.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS is also developing analytics capabilities to enhance its surveillance of FIs' market conduct practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes making better use of data from complaints, misconduct reports and regulatory returns.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All said and done, this is still necessary and is an integral part of our system to promote good corporate governance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Unlike culture, which is implicit, this is the explicit part where we have to take action when anyone flouts the rules and regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has a reputation of being a no-nonsense regulator.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will come down on FIs when lapses lead to control deficiencies, regulatory breaches or criminal offences.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not every one of these actions is published in the media but they have a salutary effect on the FIs concerned.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Other than enforcement action, there is, of course, the lighter regime of the Code of Corporate Governance, which applies to listed companies on a comply-or-explain basis that Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is timely to do so, given that we live in a rapidly evolving business and global business landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The last review was done a number of years back, in 2012.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Council consulted many stakeholders and studied the systems across various countries, including OECD Principles of Corporate Governance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of these go to the heart of what Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan has raised, including his question on how to promote responsible conduct amongst listed companies which may face pressure to show good financial performance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will continue to maintain the current arrangement where FIs that are systemically important are subject to even higher corporate governance requirements, compared to other listed companies, in terms of director independence, board composition and the establishment of specific board committees.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are also expected to comply with more stringent disclosure requirements, such as in the areas of risk management and remuneration.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in sum, getting governance, culture and conduct right is crucial to maintaining public trust in our FIs and the reputation of our financial sector.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The board and senior management have a critical role to play and, as far as FIs are concerned, MAS will continue to partner them to foster a strong culture and good practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, I have a clarification for Minister Josephine Teo.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: She has described at length and quite extensively the support measures to make Singapore a great place for families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: But are our current measures and enhancements to support Singaporeans' marriage and parenthood aspirations enough?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Because many of these incentives have been around for some years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: What else can we do to encourage young married couples to have children and, for those who already have one child, to have even more children?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I want to thank the Member Mr Melvin Yong for his question.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Earlier on, I was talking about Russia and the Order of Parental Glory.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo pointed out to me that the Order of Parental Glory that Russia has, requires seven children, before you can make it to the Kremlin to receive this Order.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But in Soviet times, actually you need 10 children in order to receive the Hero Mother of Soviet Union Award.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our package of support does not require 10 or even seven kids.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We provide quite a wide-ranging suite of schemes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The handout will show that it is quite comprehensive, and the schemes have also been progressively enhanced.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I think in addressing the question that Mr Melvin Yong brought up, it is perhaps useful for us to take a step back and ask what has happened to our TFR over a longer time horizon.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we did that, we can make two observations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, let me try and say a bit more about each one of those two observations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The sharpest decline we experienced was in the 1960s and then the 1970s.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That period coincided with rapid urbanisation as well as economic growth, and the pattern is quite similar to the developed East Asian societies and even in the Nordic countries.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second observation that TFR has stabilised around 1.2, that is also a level that is quite similar to the East Asian societies of South Korea, Taiwan, Japan.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We all developed rapidly around the same time, and it had that sort of an effect on our TFR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I shared last year during the COS debate quite extensively so I would not attempt to repeat everything in its entirety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the other hand, we must be cognisant of what could have happened without the support measures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Could it be possible that TFR in South Korea and also Singapore would have fallen further without these support measures?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What matters appears to be that, more than a package of support measures, society as a whole needs to make marriage and parenthood achievable, enjoyable and celebrated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For millennials, this is the part we are very mindful of.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think we must recognise that they have career aspirations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most of them want to remain active in the workforce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Especially for the women, there is so much more room for us to improve.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, if you let me show a slide, I hope to illustrate the point.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Yes, please, but can you keep your answers concise?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we take a look at our female labour force participation rate for Singapore, we reach the highest level up to the age of 29 and then it drops and it does not recover.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Japan actually is lower than us at the younger ages; the black one is below the red line but after the drop it recovers and there is a double hump.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It remains high, all the way up to women in their 50s.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, how do we address this in the case of Singapore?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is the reason why the current priority is: one, more preschool places near homes, near workplaces to enable women to continue working and have that peace of mind; two, sharing of parental responsibilities that Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin spoke about − more support for not just mums but also dads, more workplace support, FWAs, and I will share more during the COS debate on MOM.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can I ask if the 360-degree review will be made available to all public servants and how regularly this will be done?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Minister also respond to the idea of an internal QSM?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I do thank Minister Ong also for sharing that all public officers can speak up without fear of getting into trouble.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And I am keen to be part of the solution, which is why I spent the past year meeting, listening to and working with public officers and now share their concerns with everyone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I will take Minister Ong's advice and will be more careful about generalisations of public officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: — unpaid leave for parents of multiples or pre-term babies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But can I ask whether there are plans to legislate this?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I also have to add that after looking after twins for a year, there is no way we will have seven kids.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But 360 is largely a developmental tool − 360-degree feedback appraisal.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I do not think it is useful to extend it to all public officers but, certainly, to senior officers who are leaders, who have to work with people around them − up, sideways, down.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the issue is not really 360-degree feedback as a mechanism but to make sure that the Public Service and also the individual agencies have a culture of wanting to do better, embracing change, prepared to be innovative and to have people who do this in the right spirit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That when there is big change, they try to support it or, if they cannot support it, they get out of their way or, if they have totally different ideas, be able to voice them up, debate, come to a resolution and then support the direction forward.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think this is really about building that right organisation culture.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, likewise, it is not really about whether you have internal QSM or not, but whether the organisation believes in engaging its people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I do think I agree with Mr Louis Ng that all public agencies ought to engage their people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All public agencies today do conduct staff engagement surveys periodically.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And in that process, you do have to engage your people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, let us work together and let us all be part of the change and be part of the transformation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Since I am at the podium, Mr Chairman, I realise I did not quite answer one of Ms Sylvia Lim's clarification just now in one of her cuts where she mentioned during the Administration of Justice (Protection) Bill, her petition filed on the Bill was, I quote her, "somehow not sent to the Public Petitions Committee".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I thought I had better clear the air and "what somehow" really meant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The First Reading was July, I think 10 July.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Second Reading was 15 August 2016; I checked that this is the correct date.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The petition was filed on 10 August 2016, five days before Second Reading.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if it had come to the House on the Second Reading, it would have been referred to the next Sitting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By then, it would have been moot because we would have already had the Second Reading debate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If Members remember, a Motion was, therefore, tabled to refer the petition to Parliament as part of the Second Reading debate, instead of sending it to the Public Petitions Committee.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so, a general assent was called, everyone in the House agreed and we had a full debate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun, who filed the petition, and Ms Sylvia Lim, were also present.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Sylvia Lim had a full speech, many clarifications, long debate I remember and then also voted on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I thought it is good to clarify this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the real question is not whether we can or we cannot legislate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The real question is why, even with legislation, utilisation is not always 100%.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think that has got to do with the fact that, at workplaces, people do not always feel that they can use their entitlements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And that also has got to do with culture, whether there is a comfort that there will be no push back from the employers, that performance appraisal is not impacted, that co-workers are not unhappy because you go away.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What we have attempted to do is, when there is a new leave type, perhaps we start with a tripartite standard first.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Let the employers who are ready and willing, come on board, and then expand this group.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Because what you really need to do is to promote a new culture.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This culture of support is harder to try and bring about, but it is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Mr Chairman, one clarification to seek from Minister Josephine Teo.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Before having children, the first most important step is getting married.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I understand from an NPTD survey that was commissioned in 2016 − the Marriage and Parenthood Survey − showed that 83% of young Singaporeans want to settle down.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: However, if you look slightly further down in the survey, it is a little bit more worrying because 59% of singles are not seriously dating and 41% have never dated seriously before.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: And of those not dating seriously, 42% prefer to leave dating to chance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It means, if it comes along, it comes along.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Is there more that the Government can do to promote the environment and to encourage young Singaporeans to perhaps date more with a mind of settling down and then, eventually, having children and, perhaps, having seven children?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The short answer to that question is that I am really open to suggestions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If you know of a way in which the Government can do this without coming across like nannies and without being thought of as being very intrusive in people's private affairs, I think we are certainly keen.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Social Development Network, under the charge of MSF, continues to support the private dating scene, primarily from the point of view that this is not always something that is the Government's core competence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Expanding the network where private sector players have the right creative ideas to bring people together, that continues to be an emphasis.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I just want to reassure the Member that the Social Development Network is continuing its work.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It has not stopped its work at all.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, please keep your questions succinct and may I also ask the front bench to keep your answers short, too.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I have some residents who have approached me because of the age limit of the scheme.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, I am wondering whether the Ministry will be open to consider extending the scheme to those who are above 40 years old.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The empirical evidence for Assisted Reproduction Technology success rates is quite stark.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The challenge for the Government is that if you make the support available to those above the age of 40, it does give the impression that there is a reasonable chance for you to succeed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Otherwise, how is it that the Government can justify using taxpayers' money to subsidise this?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am directing this clarification to Minister Vivian Balakrishnan.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Earlier on, the Minister mentioned about introduction of personal biometric identifiers.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If there are no further clarifications, may I ask whether the Member Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef would wish to withdraw her amendment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: From "Moments of Life" to preschool education emplacement, to couple-hood and sub-fertility issues, also including Smart Nation, AI and even voting during the General Elections, we have discussed it all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: We thank the Deputy Prime Minister and all the Ministers who have responded to our questions vividly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Also, we look forward to the journey together with our Public Service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: We would like to thank all our Public Service officers who have been working really hard, researching and also putting at top form our Public Service in Singapore that is well-known globally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: We look forward to the journey that we will take with them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Mr Chairman, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
